sens: A person in servitude, without freedom, owned by a master
A servant employed by a master, who obeys him
A state of dependence, subjugation to someone or something
One who belongs to God or Christ by covenant and obedience
One who is dominated by sin or by a passion
G1401.detail:
1. A slave is a person who does not have their freedom: they belong to a master who owns and controls them. This is the state opposed to that of a free man. The Apostle Paul refers to this real state by saying: "Were you called while a slave? Do not be concerned about it" (1 Corinthians 7:21), acknowledging that some Christians were born into this condition.

2. The master employs his servant to carry out his orders and tasks. The Roman officer recounts: "I have soldiers under my command; and I say to one, 'Go!' and he goes; and to another, 'Come!' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this!' and he does it" (Matthew 8:9). The servant does entirely what he is commanded.

3. To enslave also means to become dependent, submissive to a force that controls us. Paul writes: "You have become slaves of sin" (Romans 6:16) — the image is one of voluntary captivity.

4. In the New Testament, believers describe themselves as "servants of God" or "servants of Christ": not humiliated, but honored to belong to the one they love. Titus is presented as a "servant of God" (Titus 1:1). It is the obedience of love, not coercion.

5. The man without Christ is a "slave to sin": he believes he is free, but he obeys a master who destroys him. Jesus says: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin" (John 8:34). This servitude is spiritual but real.
G1401.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient root meaning one who is bound, enslaved. In Hebrew, the word עֶבֶד (eved) means both slave and servant: the Old Testament uses it for both slaves in the strict sense and for great servants of God, like Abraham or Moses, who referred to themselves as the "servants" of the Lord. The Greek word δοῦλος translates this rich Hebrew notion exactly.
G1401.emploi: The word appears more than 120 times in the New Testament. It primarily refers to slaves in the concrete sense: the servants of masters in parables (Matthew 18:23, Luke 20:10), or historical figures like the servant of the centurion (Matthew 8:9, Luke 7:8). Paul uses it to describe the real condition of Christians who were slaves in his time (1 Corinthians 7:21). But the New Testament transforms the meaning: the apostles proclaim themselves as "servants of God" or "servants of Christ" (Romans 1:1, Titus 1:1, James 1:1), giving this word a spiritual dignity. Furthermore, Paul speaks of humans as "slaves of sin" (Romans 6:16-17, John 8:34) to show that sin enslaves those who commit it. The word thus expresses both voluntary obedience to the Lord and involuntary subjugation to evil.
G1401.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals a paradoxical truth: serving God does not mean losing one's freedom, but finding it. One who attaches themselves to God as a servant to the Lord escapes the servitude of sin. At the same time, the word confronts us with reality: we are always enslaved to something or someone — the issue is choosing our master. Paul makes this appeal: "Do not yield your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness" (Romans 6:19). It is a call to true freedom.

sens: To reduce someone to slavery, to make them a forced servant
To put under the domination of something or someone
To voluntarily submit, to become a servant of a cause or a person
G1402.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to reduce a person to servitude, to enslave them by force. This is what the Old Testament states when it recounts that the descendants of Abraham "will be enslaved" in Egypt (Acts 7:6). It is physical slavery, the loss of freedom.

2. The verb also describes a moral or spiritual domination: to be enslaved to something means to become its slave without having chosen it. Before knowing Christ, humans are enslaved to sin, to wine, to the elements of the world (Galatians 4:3) — these are not visible chains, but a servitude just as real.

3. The word can also express a voluntary and positive submission. Paul says that he has become "a servant to all" to win souls (1 Corinthians 9:19), and he exhorts believers to become "slaves of righteousness" and "slaves of God" (Romans 6:18, 6:22). Here, one freely chooses to serve a good cause.
G1402.origine: The verb comes from δοῦλος (doulos), "slave." In Hebrew, the word that the Greek Bible translates as douloō is עָבַד (avad), which primarily means "to serve" or "to work," then "to be enslaved." The root evokes the idea of forced labor and dependence. The Greek word retains this dual meaning: imposed slavery and voluntary service.
G1402.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It first refers to historical enslavement (Egypt: Acts 7:6), then it is used metaphorically to describe spiritual servitude. In Paul, the contrast is striking: believers are "freed from sin" to become "slaves of righteousness" and "slaves of God" (Romans 6:18, 6:22). It is a change of master, not the absence of a master. The verb is also used to express voluntary submission (Paul becomes a servant to all: 1 Corinthians 9:19) or regrettable dependence (older women must not be "enslaved to wine": Titus 2:3). In 1 Corinthians 7:15, "bound" translates a form of the passive: not being chained by a marriage to a non-believer.
G1402.portee: This word reveals a central biblical truth: humans are never truly free to serve no one. Before Christ, one is enslaved to sin and death. By grace, one moves from a destructive servitude to a liberating servitude: becoming a slave of righteousness and of God means regaining true freedom and eternal life. For the believer, it is also a call to inner freedom: to refuse any servitude to passions (wine, lust) and consciously choose to serve what is good and just.

sens: A large public meal offered to several people
A banquet, a reception
A celebration through the table and food
G1403.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a large meal to which many people are invited. When Levi becomes a disciple of Jesus, he organizes a feast in his house to introduce him to his friends (Luke 5:29): it is a generous and joyful table celebration that gathers the community. 2. The feast is also an occasion for moral generosity. Jesus teaches: "When you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind" (Luke 14:13). The word then evokes not only the meal itself but the act of conviviality and sharing that it represents. 3. By extension, the feast symbolizes communion, shared joy, and in the Bible, often divine blessing and brotherhood.
G1403.origine: The Greek word δοχή comes from the verb δέχομαι (to receive, to welcome): a feast is primarily what is received, what is offered to you. It translates the Hebrew מִשְׁתֶּה (mishté, "banquet"), which has the same root as the word "to drink": in the ancient Near East, the banquet is inseparable from drink, fruits, and the pleasures of the table. It is a word of hospitality and abundance.
G1403.emploi: The word appears twice in the Gospel of Luke, in two different but complementary contexts. First, Levi organizes a feast to welcome Jesus and his disciples into his home, mixing his former fellow tax collectors with the new community of disciples (Luke 5:29). Then, Jesus uses the word to ethically redefine what a true feast is: not a meal among the rich or among friends of the same rank, but a table open to the poor and the infirm (Luke 14:13). The word thus shifts from an ordinary social event to a practice of justice and charity.
G1403.portee: The word feast reminds the Christian that the table is a place of revelation: it is at the table that Jesus makes himself known, that he blesses, that he teaches. Inviting to meals is living the gospel. Jesus also corrects a common practice — the exclusivity of aristocratic banquets — by introducing love for the poor and weak neighbor. The feast becomes a parable of the Church: an open, generous communion, transformed by the presence of Christ.

sens: Mythological creature that is terrifying with multiple heads and horns
Symbolic representation of Satan and his evil forces
G1404.detail:
1. In mythological language, the dragon is a fabulous, immense, and monstrous beast: in Revelation 12:3, John describes it with seven heads and ten horns, a being of superhuman power that causes terror. This is the raw image of the word.
2. In John's vision, this dragon becomes the figure of Satan himself and his opposition to God. In Revelation 12:9, the dragon is explicitly identified as "the ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan." The word then symbolizes organized malice, rebellion against God, and the destructive power of evil. Revelation 13:4 shows that some worship this dragon, actually worshiping Satan beyond appearances.
G1404.origine: The Greek word δράκων comes from an ancient root evoking the idea of "that which looks fixedly" or "that which sees clearly" — the dragon is a gaze, an evil vigilance. In biblical Hebrew, the word תַּנִּין (tanin) sometimes refers to the dragon or monstrous crocodile. The dragon is also rooted in the imagery of the ancient Near East, where this cosmic monster symbolizes chaos and opposition to the divine.
G1404.emploi: The word "dragon" appears only in Revelation, in twelve passages. John uses it exclusively to speak of Satan and his manifestations. Revelation 12 depicts a cosmic conflict: the dragon pursues the woman (the Church) and seeks to devour her child, then makes war on the believers (12:13, 12:17). In Revelation 13, the dragon gives its authority to the beast, this anti-divine political power that men worship. In chapter 16, unclean spirits come out of the mouth of the dragon. Finally, in Revelation 20:2, the angel chains and seals the dragon for a thousand years. The image remains consistent: Satan under the guise of a hostile power, visible or invisible, but always defeated or destined to be.
G1404.portee: For the Christian reader, the dragon reveals the hidden spiritual reality behind the events of the world: there is an invisible battle waged by Satan against the Church and the faithful. But Revelation also teaches that this dragon has no ultimate power: he is thrown down, his angels are defeated, and his reign comes to an end. The word thus invites clarity in the face of evil and confidence in the final victory of Christ.

sens: To seize with the hand, to catch something or someone
To capture, to trap, to put someone in a position where they cannot escape
In a figurative sense: to catch someone in their own game, to confuse them by their own cunning
G1405.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to seize something or someone with the hand, to catch firmly. It is a concrete gesture: one closes the hand around an object or grabs a person. This verb translates into Greek the Hebrew idea of seizing or pinching.

2. To capture or trap means to catch someone in such a way that they cannot escape: one "takes" a prisoner, one "takes" someone in a trap. The emphasis here is on immobilization, rendering someone unable to harm or escape.

3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, the verb denotes the act of confusing someone by their own cunning, to "take" them in the nets of their own trap. In 1 Corinthians 3:19, Paul writes that God "takes the wise in their craftiness": he confounds them by turning their own malice against them, like a hunter who captures an animal in the trap he has set himself.
G1405.origine: The verb δράσσομαι comes from a Greek root expressing the action of closing the hand on something, of seizing firmly. In the Greek Old Testament, it notably translates the Hebrew נָשַׁק ("to kiss," but in the sense of seizing with force) and קָמַץ ("to pinch," "to take a handful"). These two Hebrew roots evoke a concrete manual action: the hand that closes, that grips, that holds.
G1405.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Corinthians 3:19. Paul cites a passage from Psalm 94:11 (freely translated according to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament), applying this word to divine action. God is not deceived by false human wisdom; he "takes" it — he confounds it, he masters it — by turning it against those who devised it. The Pauline context, where he denounces divisions and false doctrines in the church of Corinth, shows that the word carries a judgmental weight here: those who think themselves wise by turning away from Christ ultimately find themselves captured by their own folly.
G1405.portee: This word reminds us that God is not fooled by human malice. When someone weaves a web of cunning or lies, they believe they are acting in secret, but God sees, God judges, and he "takes" — he confounds — these plots at the hour when only he knows. For the reader, this is an assurance: true wisdom consists in trusting Christ and the word of God rather than the false wisdom of the world, for the latter always leads to being trapped by one's own folly.

sens: Greek silver coin
Unit of value equivalent to the Roman denarius
Daily wage of a worker
G1406.detail:
1. The drachma is a silver coin used in the Greek world. It is the Greek equivalent of the Roman denarius: a small coin of moderate value, neither precious nor insignificant. In the parable of Luke 15, a woman has ten drachmas and loses one, which justifies her efforts to find it — it is enough to worry her, but not enough to be ruined.
2. Economically, the drachma represents roughly the daily wage of a worker or a laborer. It thus measures a modest wealth, that of ordinary people: sufficient to live, fragile to lose.
3. Figuratively, each drachma symbolizes in the parable something precious despite its modest price — here, perhaps a lost soul that God seeks with ardor, suggesting that none is negligible in His eyes.
G1406.origine: The Greek word δραχμή comes from a root meaning "to seize" or "to take with full fingers": the drachma was the amount of coins that could be held in one hand. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew שֶׁקֶל (shekel) and other monetary terms. It is a unit of weight measurement before becoming a minted coin.
G1406.emploi: The word δραχμή appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke 15:8-9, in the parable of the woman who lost a coin. Luke uses it to give the narrative an ordinary, popular tone: it is not a huge sum, but a real sum, that of a woman of modest means. The repeated use (ten drachmas, then the lost drachma) emphasizes the importance of what seems small: each coin counts, each unit is sought after with care. It is a parable about the joy of finding what was lost.
G1406.portee: The drachma reminds us that God cares for each one, even for those who seem insignificant in the eyes of the world. The modest economic price of the coin does not prevent the woman from searching for it earnestly, nor does it prevent Jesus from constructing an entire parable around its loss: an invitation to recognize the infinite value of each soul before God.

sens: Harvesting tool with a curved, sharp blade
Instrument of divine judgment in prophetic visions
G1407.detail:
1. The sickle is a simple agricultural tool: a curved, sharp blade attached to a short handle, used to cut wheat ears or grape clusters at harvest. In Mark 4:29, Jesus describes the growth of the kingdom of God using the imagery of harvest: "As soon as the fruit is ripe, he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
2. In Revelation, the sickle becomes the instrument of divine judgment at the end of times. The heavenly angels hold it to execute judgment: one harvests the wheat (the gathering of believers), while the other gathers the vine of the earth (the judgment of the wicked) in Revelation 14:14-18. Christ himself, seated on a cloud, holds a "sharp" sickle to harvest the earth.
G1407.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient form (δρεπάνη) associated with the verb δρέπω ("to gather, to pluck"). It is related to δρέπω which means "pluck, gather" and expresses the idea of harvesting by cutting. The Hebrew word חֶרְמֵשׁ ("sickle") is rendered by this term in the ancient Greek translations of the Old Testament.
G1407.emploi: The word appears 7 times, concentrated in two key passages. In Mark 4:29, Jesus uses it once in the parable of the mustard seed to refer to the moment when the harvest is ready. In Revelation 14:14-19, the word appears 6 times in a succession of visions: four distinct angels appear, three with a sharp sickle, executing the final judgments of the Lord. The sickle thus transitions from an ordinary agricultural context to an eschatological symbol of divine judgment and the separation between the elect and the reprobate.
G1407.portee: For the believer, the sickle serves as a reminder that God's harvest is approaching. In Mark 4, it assures that the kingdom of God is reaching maturity and will soon be harvested. In Revelation, it invites the reader to recognize that the final judgment is the certain work of Christ: the earth will be judged according to divine justice, believers will be gathered, and injustice will be removed. This symbolism urges vigilance and faith in God's ultimate victory.

sens: Course que doit accomplir un coureur dans une compétition
Mission ou ministère conçu comme un parcours à compléter
Vie entière vue comme un chemin à parcourir jusqu'à son terme
G1408.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a race in the literal sense, a course that the runner must complete — an image drawn from the athletic games of the time. 2. It is used figuratively to denote the mission that God entrusts to someone, a ministry that must be carried out from beginning to end. Acts 20:24 speaks of "my race" to signify the ministry received from the Lord. 3. More broadly, it is life itself viewed as a course with a start and finish, a task to be completed before stopping. Paul in 2 Timothy 4:7 summarizes his entire life by saying, "I have finished the race," a powerful image of a life well-lived to the end.
G1408.origine: The word comes from the verb meaning to run or to hasten (related to trecho). In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew merkouza, which also denotes a race. The word thus initially evokes the physical effort of the runner covering a distance, then extends to any course, any mission that must be completed.
G1408.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a figurative sense. In Paul, it describes ministry as a task to be accomplished: John the Baptist "finishes his race" (Acts 13:25) by fulfilling his role as forerunner, Paul wants to "complete his race with joy" by proclaiming the Gospel (Acts 20:24), and at the end of his life, he asserts that he has "finished the race" (2 Timothy 4:7). The word always retains the idea of progression toward completion.
G1408.portee: This image of a race helps the Christian to see life as a mission, not a vague journey. It invites perseverance and faithfulness to the end, like Paul who finishes his race with joy. It also shows that God assigns each person a specific role to fulfill, a "race" that is uniquely theirs, and that relying on Christ provides the strength to complete it.

sens: wife of the Roman governor Felix
G1409.detail: Drusilla is the wife of the Roman governor Felix, who rules over Judea in the 50s-60s. Although she is a non-Jew by birth, she converted to Judaism and married Felix. She is the one who accompanies him when he brings the apostle Paul in Acts 24:24 to listen to him speak about faith in Christ.
G1409.origine: Drusilla is a Roman feminine name, attested in patrician families. The historical context shows that she is Drusilla, daughter of Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II, important figures in first-century Palestinian Judaism.
G1409.emploi: Drusilla appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 24:24. She is present at a crucial moment in the narrative: Paul is in detention in Caesarea, and Felix summons him with Drusilla to hear him preach about faith in Christ. Her presence underscores the couple's interest in religious matters, even though the text does not indicate how they will react to Paul's preaching.
G1409.portee: The mention of Drusilla reminds us that the Gospel was heard by high-ranking figures, both Roman and Jewish. It illustrates how the Word of God addressed all levels of society, including the powerful of the time.

sens: To have the physical or intellectual capacity to do something
To have permission or authority to do something
To have the opportunity or favorable circumstances to do something
To be possible, achievable
To have the legitimate right to do something
To possess the necessary power or strength
G1410.detail:
1. To have physical or intellectual capacity: this means being able to accomplish an action, to realize it concretely. A child "cannot" lift a stone that is too heavy, or someone "cannot" understand a word without God's help (Luke 1:20: Zechariah cannot speak until Elizabeth gives birth).
2. To have permission or authority: this means having the recognized right to do something. No one has the "right" to deliver Paul to his accusers if he has not committed the crime (Acts 25:11).
3. To have the opportunity or favorable circumstances: this means that the conditions allow for the action. Jesus "cannot" come with his disciples to the wedding feast because the time has not yet come (Matthew 9:15).
4. To be possible, achievable: the intended action is not against nature or against the laws. From stones, God "can" raise up children for Abraham (Matthew 3:9) — what seems impossible becomes possible.
5. To have the legitimate right: this is the moral or legal foundation of an action. In John 8:21, the disciples "cannot" go where Jesus is going, not due to lack of strength, but because they are dying in sin and do not have the right.
6. To possess power or strength: this means having within oneself the capacity to act effectively. With God, all things are possible (Matthew 19:26).
G1410.origine: The verb δύναμαι comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to be strong" or "to have strength"; it is found in the noun δύναμις ("power, strength"). In Greek, it is used for all types of capacity: physical, moral, legal, or divine. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew יָכֹל (yakol), which means "to be able" or "to have the strength to." This verb thus expresses the fundamental idea that "to be able" is to have within oneself the strength, permission, or opportunity to accomplish something.
G1410.emploi: δύναμαι appears nearly 200 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It pertains to all areas: ordinary human action (to be able to rise, to be able to eat), human limitations (one cannot serve two masters, Matthew 6:24), miracles (God can raise up children, Matthew 3:9), and spiritual life (one cannot enter the Kingdom without being born again, John 3:3). The meaning nuances according to the context: with an infinitive ("I can do"), it expresses actual capacity; in the absolute ("I can"), it asserts power in general; in the negative, it marks impossibility or prohibition. The Gospels often use it to show what Jesus "can" do (heal, forgive) and what the disciples "cannot" do without him.
G1410.portee: This verb reminds us that all ability ultimately comes from God: we "can" do nothing without him (John 15:5). It invites the reader to discern between carnal power (which deceives) and the power of the Spirit. It also shows us the limits of our nature: we "cannot" save ourselves, we "cannot" serve two masters, but with God all things become possible. For the Christian, understanding what the Bible says about "power" illuminates dependence on God and the freedom he gives us through grace.

sens: Strength, vigor, capacity to act or accomplish something
Ability to perform an action, potential
Manifestation of a force in action, visible effect
Miracle, extraordinary act revealing superhuman power
Authority, dominion, reign
Being or power personified (God, angel, army)
G1411.detail:
1. Power is primarily a raw force, a capacity: it is the energy one possesses, like the talents that a master distributes to his servants according to their abilities (Matthew 25:15). It is also the physical strength that manifests when a healthy person differs from a weakened sick person (1 Corinthians 15:43).

2. It is also the capacity to do something, to accomplish a task: Peter and John ask "by what power or in whose name" the authorities perform miracles (Acts 4:7). It is the skill, know-how, the resources one can mobilize.

3. When this force acts visibly, it becomes power in action: the Holy Spirit clothes the disciples with power from on high to testify (Luke 24:49), and the Gospel itself is the power of God for salvation (Romans 1:16).

4. Power often manifests through miracles — extraordinary acts that surpass natural laws: Jesus performs miracles (Mark 6:2), and his disciples also do so in his name (Mark 9:39). These astonishing gestures reveal a force that comes from elsewhere.

5. Power can also refer to authority, the right to command: the Son of Man is seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69), meaning at the place of divine power and reign.

6. By extension, the word designates beings that exercise this power: God himself (Matthew 26:64), angels (Romans 8:38), or entire armies (Luke 21:26 speaks of the powers of heaven).
G1411.origine: The Greek word δύναμις comes from the root δύνα-, which expresses capacity, possibility: it is "what one is capable of." In Hebrew, it often translates גְבוּרָה (strength) or חַיִל (strength, army), and related words. The verb δύναμαι means "to be able," "to be capable of" — power is its noun form, the state or quality. It is power as capacity, in contrast to other Greek words like κράτος (absolute dominion) or ἐξουσία (legal authority).
G1411.emploi: The word appears 116 times in the New Testament, everywhere except in the epistles of John. It is particularly frequent in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Paul. In the first three Gospels, it primarily refers to the miracles of Jesus and his power to act: his power heals and casts out demons (Luke 4:36), or remains suspended when faith is lacking (Mark 6:5). Paul uses it to speak of the power of the Gospel (Romans 1:16), the resurrection power of Christ (Romans 1:4), or the power of God that acts through faith (1 Corinthians 1:24 calls Christ "the power of God"). In doxologies, it glorifies the Lord (Matthew 6:13: "For yours is the power and the glory"). The word can also refer to someone's capacity — notably financial capacity (2 Corinthians 8:3) or the gift of performing miracles (1 Corinthians 12:10).
G1411.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life is not primarily a matter of human will, but of divine power in action. Jesus acts with a power that nothing stops except our unbelief (Mark 6:5). The Gospel itself is not a beautiful theory, but a living power that liberates and transforms. For the believer, seeking divine power rather than human resources is to place one's trust in the true source of change and salvation.

sens: Make strong, give physical or moral strength
Strengthen someone in a capacity, virtue, or conviction
G1412.detail:
1. The word literally means "to make powerful": to give someone the strength, vigor, or ability to accomplish what requires effort. It is the action of reinforcing a being or a quality within them. In Hebrews 11:34, believers from the Old Testament "were healed of their diseases" — their bodies received the power to recover.
2. In a moral and spiritual sense, to fortify means to strengthen someone in a virtue or conviction, making them capable of standing firm and persevering. In Colossians 1:11, Paul prays that believers be "strengthened in every way by His glorious power, so that you may have great endurance and patience, joyfully giving thanks" — God strengthens them to stand firm in faith and endurance.
G1412.origine: The word comes from δύναμις (dynamis), which means "power" or "strength." The root expresses the idea of an ability to act, a power put into action. In Hebrew, the word often translates עָזַז ("to become strong") or גָּבַר ("to prevail, be mighty"), which share this image of strength or vigor acquired or reinforced.
G1412.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Colossians 1:11, Paul uses it to describe how God spiritually strengthens believers through His glorious power, so that they may persevere with joy and patience. In Hebrews 11:34, in recalling the exploits of faith, the word denotes how saints from the Old Testament were strengthened to heal from diseases, conquer in battle, and flee armies. In both cases, it is God or His power that fortifies, never man by his own strength.
G1412.portee: This word reminds the believer that true strength, which matters in spiritual life and moral endurance, does not come from oneself but from God. It invites one to place their trust in divine "glorious power" rather than in their own resources, and assures that God can fortify, heal, and strengthen those who believe in Him, no matter the trial.

sens: One who possesses power, authority, dominion
A high dignitary, an officer of great authority in the service of a king
One who reigns, the absolute sovereign
G1413.detail:
1. The powerful one is one who has power and authority: it is someone who dominates, who governs. Mary in her song praises God who "has brought down the mighty from their thrones" (Luke 1:52) — she speaks of those kings and great ones of this world who believed they ruled by their strength.
2. The word also designates a high official, a state minister who exercises power in the name of a king. The Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8:27 is a "minister" of Queen Candace — a chief who controls royal wealth and enjoys great authority.
3. In the highest sense, it is the sovereign himself, the one who reigns without sharing. Paul calls Christ "the sovereign," the only one who truly possesses eternal power (1 Timothy 6:15).
G1413.origine: The word comes from the verb δύναμαι (to be able, to be capable), which evokes strength and the ability to act. A powerful one is etymologically one who "can," who has the capacity and the right to command. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew גִּבּוֹר ("warrior, strong man") and other terms denoting authority. The word family includes δύναμις (power, strength) and δυνατός (powerful, possible).
G1413.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament in three distinct contexts that illuminate its scope. In Luke 1:52, it refers to the powerful of the world, the earthly authorities that God can bring down — it is the sense of one who dominates by human strength. In Acts 8:27, it is a high official, a royal steward in charge of the treasury, showing that the word applies to the man of power, the influential dignitary. In 1 Timothy 6:15, applied to God and Christ, it takes on its full value: it is the absolute sovereign, the only true master — no human powerful one can be compared to Him.
G1413.portee: This word reminds the Christian that true power belongs to God alone. All the powerful of this world, all human authorities, are nothing before His eternal sovereignty. It is a comfort for those who suffer injustice: God can bring down oppressors. It is also a call to humility: to recognize that our own authority, however great, is fragile and limited compared to the reign of Christ.

sens: To have the capacity, strength, or authority to do something
To be capable, competent for an action
To be powerful, endowed with remarkable strength or power
G1414.detail: 1. The primary meaning is the practical capacity to accomplish an action: to be able to do something, to have the means and strength. This is what Paul expresses in Romans 14:4 when he says that the Lord "has the power to uphold him" — He has the capacity and strength. 2. This power can also mean having authority or right over something: in Romans 14:4, the French verb "look" translates a nuance where it concerns what depends on someone, their competence or domain. 3. Finally, the word expresses strength, power in itself: in 2 Corinthians 13:3, Christ is "powerful" among the Corinthians, meaning He manifests His real and active power. In 2 Corinthians 9:8, God "can" fill you — His divine power gives Him absolute capacity.
G1414.origine: The word comes from the adjective dunatos (capable, powerful), itself derived from dunamis, the classical Greek word for power, strength, energy — the very word Paul uses to speak of the "power of God." The verb δυνατέω literally means "to be in a state of power or capacity." This root expresses not only brute strength but an effective capacity, a power that can act and produce results.
G1414.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all occurrences found in Paul's epistles. In Romans 14:4, Paul uses it to affirm that it is the Lord who has the authority and capacity to support a weak believer in his faith. In 2 Corinthians 9:8, it expresses divine capacity: God can abundantly fill you with grace. In 2 Corinthians 13:3, the word describes the manifested power of Christ among the church. In all cases, the context concerns divine power or that of the risen Christ — it is a supernatural power, not mere human competence.
G1414.portee: This word reminds the reader that true power belongs to God and Christ. It invites us to rest our trust not on our own strengths, but on God's ability to support, fill, and transform us. It is a word of encouragement: the God who "can" fill us with grace and strengthen us is not a distant creator, but an active Father, whose power works on behalf of His children. For the believer, this power is never out of reach, as it is already at work among His own.

sens: That can be realized, that is feasible
Capable of doing something
That has strength, power
That possesses the means or authority to act
G1415.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of what can happen or be done: "With God, all things are possible" (Matthew 19:26), in contrast to human limitations. It conveys the idea that there are no obstacles for it to be realized.

2. The word also describes someone who has the capacity, strength, or competence to accomplish a specific action: "if it were possible for him" to be in Jerusalem (Acts 20:16), or someone who is "able" to keep what has been entrusted to him (2 Timothy 1:12).

3. It qualifies strength, power, or authority, particularly in the spiritual realm: the Corinthians are "strong" in faith when Paul is weak (2 Corinthians 13:9), or Stephen was "mighty in words" (Acts 7:22).

4. It also refers to one who possesses power or mastery, the "mighty" men in Acts 25:5 being the authorities capable of deciding and acting.
G1415.origine: The word comes from the root δύναμαι, which fundamentally means "to be able, to have strength." This root evokes the idea of available power, of potential at work. The Greek word translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew terms גִּבּוֹר (mighty, hero) and חַיִל (strength, valor), showing that the Bible connects possibility and power to the notion of a force that acts.
G1415.emploi: The word appears approximately 32 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It has three main nuances: 1) In the neutral form, δυνατόν means "possible" and qualifies what can be done (Matthew 19:26, Luke 18:27, Acts 20:16) — this is the most frequent usage. 2) In the masculine or feminine form, it qualifies a person as "mighty" or "able," either in physical or political strength (Acts 25:5: the leaders), or in spiritual strength (2 Corinthians 13:9: you are strong). 3) With an infinitive, it expresses the capacity to do: "able to do" (2 Timothy 1:12, Hebrews 11:19). The nuance evolves from the general sense of "possible" to the more personal sense of "capable," depending on the context.
G1415.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the limits of their own power and that of God. When Jesus says, "With God, all things are possible," it frees one from anxiety in the face of human impossibility and grounds faith in divine power. For the Christian, "being strong" or "capable" in Christ also becomes a promise: God gives spiritual power to those who rely on Him, transforming incapacity into strength.

sens: To plunge into, to sink into
To disappear below the horizon (referring to the sun)
G1416.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to "sink" or "plunge" into something, like an object gradually sinking into a medium. It is an image of downward or inward movement.
2. The main meaning in the New Testament is "to set" or "to disappear below the horizon," specifically applied to the sun. In Mark 1:32 and Luke 4:40, the word denotes the moment of sunset: "after the sun had set," that is, when the sun goes down below the horizon and the day ends. This image is very concrete: the sun that "sinks" is exactly what everyone observes every evening.
G1416.origine: The word δύνω is an Ionic (Greek dialect) and tragic form of δύω. It shares the root δύ-, which evokes the idea of entering or sinking. This same root appears in several compounds such as ἐκδύνω ("to strip off"), ἀποδύνω ("to sink away"), ἐνδύνω ("to sink into"), and ἐπιδύνω ("to sink upon"). In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew verb בּוֹא ("to enter, to go"), although in these passages of the New Testament it pertains to the specific image of sunset.
G1416.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the Synoptics and always concerning the setting sun. In Mark 1:32 and Luke 4:40, it marks the transition from day to night, the moment when the sun disappears below the horizon. These two passages are parallel: both situate the arrival of the sick to Jesus at sunset, indicating that people were waiting for the end of work (it was the Sabbath) to approach Jesus. The word has only one meaning in these two usages: the astronomical and observable sense of sunset.
G1416.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospels pay attention to natural rhythms and the hours of the day. The setting sun is not just a notation of time: it is a moment of transition, where day becomes night, where the constraints of the Sabbath end, and where the sick can finally present themselves to Jesus. This attention to concrete details — an hour, a season, a light — shows that the Incarnation of Jesus unfolds in the real and observable time of this world.

sens: The number that comes after one and before three
Two people or two things together
Two groups or two parts of a whole
Distributed by two, two at a time
G1417.detail:
1. The cardinal number 2, which simply designates quantity or counting: five sparrows for two cents (Luke 12:6), a young boy who has five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:9).

2. Two people or two beings in relation: Jesus saw two brothers, Simon and Andrew (Matthew 4:18), or the idea of the couple uniting two people into one flesh (Mark 10:8).

3. Two parts of a whole that divides: the temple curtain was torn in two (Matthew 27:51), or a matter established on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Matthew 18:16).

4. A distribution: two by two, that is, in pairs, in groups of two (Mark 6:7, where Jesus sent his disciples two by two).

5. An opposition: serving two masters means being divided between two incompatible loyalties (Luke 16:13).
G1417.origine: The Greek word δύο comes from a common ancient Indo-European root shared with French "deux," Latin "duo," and other languages in this family. In Hebrew, the equivalent is שְׁנַיִם (shenaim). This word is a cardinal numeral adjective, invariable in Greek except in the dative, which agrees with the gender and number of the noun it accompanies.
G1417.emploi: The word δύο appears 122 times in the Greek New Testament, concentrated mainly in the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in the epistles of Paul. It is used to count objects (loaves, fish, talents), people (disciples, brothers, witnesses), or abstract concepts (masters, testaments). Its distributive use ("two by two" or "in pairs") is common to describe how Jesus sends his disciples on mission (Luke 10:1, Mark 6:7). The expression "two become one flesh" carries fundamental theological significance regarding marriage (Matthew 19:5-6, Mark 10:8). The word retains its literal concrete meaning throughout, never slipping into a figurative abstraction.
G1417.portee: The number two, however ordinary it may seem, carries spiritual weight in Scripture. The image of two becoming one flesh illuminates the mystery of the marital union intended by God. The sending of the disciples two by two also teaches the strength of common testimony and mutual edification. Knowing that the Lord gives weight to every detail, even numerical, helps the believer see the coherence and divine wisdom throughout all of Scripture.

sens: Difficult to carry or lift due to its weight
That weighs heavily on the one who carries it
That requires considerable, overwhelming effort
G1419.detail:
1. In the literal sense, this word describes an object that has so much weight that it can only be lifted or carried with difficulty. Jesus reproaches the religious leaders for placing on people's shoulders "heavy burdens" (Matthew 23:4) — commandments and practices that crush the faithful.
2. The word evokes the image of a weight that bears down on someone: it exceeds their strength. In Luke 11:46, the reproach is the same: the teachers of the law "load men with burdens hard to bear."
3. In a figurative sense, what is heavy is not only physically burdensome but also oppressive and unbearable — it is a moral and spiritual burden, a load imposed on others without sharing the effort.
G1419.origine: The word is composed of the prefix dus ("bad," "difficulty") and bastazô ("to carry," "to lift"). The starting image is that of a bearer struggling under the weight: du (mal) + bastazô (to carry) = what is hard to carry, what cannot be carried well. It is an adjective formed to express physical and moral difficulty.
G1419.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Jesus' words against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and the teachers of the law. In Matthew 23:4, Jesus describes the burdens that religious leaders impose on the faithful as heavy — a load too great. In Luke 11:46, he repeats the same reproach with almost the same words. Both passages aim at the same reproach: the religious authorities add commandments and practices (oral laws, traditions) that overwhelm the people, while they themselves refuse to contribute to them.
G1419.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to discern between a living faith — the Gospel of grace — and a religious system burdened with human traditions. Jesus teaches that true faith should not be an overwhelming burden imposed by leaders who do not bear it themselves. It is a call to freedom in Christ and to mercy.

sens: Severe intestinal disease characterized by inflammation and digestive disorders
Condition that renders the patient bedridden and unable to carry out their activities
G1420.detail:
1. Dysentery is an infectious disease of the intestine that causes severe inflammation, pain, and serious digestive disorders. It is a formidable condition in the ancient world, where it can be fatal without care. In Acts 28:8, Publius' father suffers from it and must remain in bed.
2. This disease renders the sufferer completely immobilized and dependent: it is mentioned alongside fever as a major affliction that keeps the patient bedridden. The healing act that Paul performs by laying on hands shows the urgency and seriousness of this condition.
G1420.origine: The Greek word δυσεντερία (dusenteria) comes from the prefix δυς- (dus-, "bad, difficult") and the noun ἔντερον (enteron, "intestine"). It literally designates the "bad state of the intestines." This word follows the rules of Greek medical terminology and describes a reality well known to physicians of antiquity, particularly in the Mediterranean and North Africa where the warm climate favors intestinal infections.
G1420.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:8. Paul and his companions have just arrived in Malta after a shipwreck. There he meets Publius, a prominent man, whose father suffers from both fever and dysentery. Paul visits him, prays for him, lays hands on him, and heals him. This event, presented as a miracle, demonstrates the power of the Gospel in the face of illness and leads the people of the island to seek Paul to be healed of their diseases.
G1420.portee: The mention of this concrete and deadly disease emphasizes that the Gospel does not operate in the abstract: Jesus and his servants heal real diseases that cause genuine suffering. It also reminds us that faith in Christ is expressed in the concrete act of intercession and laying on of hands, tangible signs of compassion toward the suffering.

sens: That requires effort to be interpreted or understood
That is obscure or confusing in its meaning
That is delicate to elucidate clearly
G1421.detail:
1. The word first evokes something that resists explanation, that does not easily translate into clear words. It is the image of a complex reality that cannot be simply expressed. In Hebrews 5:11, the apostle says that certain truths about Christ's priesthood are "difficult to explain": not false or bad, but requiring time, attention, and a certain spiritual maturity to be grasped.
2. The word can also describe what is obscure or opaque in its meaning, what is hidden beneath veils. A word difficult to explain is not transparent; it requires digging, reflecting to extract its deep meaning.
G1421.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "dus" (hard, difficult) and "hermèneutès" (interpreter, one who explains). The root "hermêneuô" itself refers to Hermes, the messenger god, and the idea of interpreting and conveying a message. Together, the word paints the image of an interpretation that resists, of an explanation that poses difficulty.
G1421.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 5:11. The author of the letter to the Hebrews uses it to qualify certain teachings of Christ: they are not impossible to understand, but they require a capacity for listening and a disposition of heart that his readers have not yet developed. The context shows that this difficulty comes less from the word itself than from the one who listens: spiritually fatigued, inattentive.
G1421.portee: This word reminds us that spiritual growth is not automatic. Understanding the depths of God's word and the mystery of Christ requires attention, perseverance, and a heart willing to learn. What is difficult to explain is never inaccessible: it is a call to move beyond spiritual passivity and indolence.

sens: That is hard to satisfy, inconvenient (about a person)
That presents a difficulty, that requires effort (about a thing or situation)
G1422.detail:
1. The word first designates a person who is hard to satisfy, who cannot be easily pleased — particularly someone who is not easy at mealtime. It is a very concrete image: one who hesitates to eat what is offered. By extension, it describes any person who is inconvenient, demanding, and difficult to align with oneself.
2. Applied to things or situations, the word means that it is hard, complicated, requiring much effort to achieve. In Mark 10:24, Jesus uses it regarding entering the kingdom of God: it is difficult for one who trusts in riches to turn to God and follow his reign.
G1422.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "dys" (δύς), which means "bad" or "difficulty," and "kolon" (κόλον), which refers to food. The starting image is thus a person "poorly fed" or "poorly satisfied by food," someone difficult at the table. The opposite Greek word is "euklos" (εὔκολος), formed from the same "kolon" preceded by the prefix "eu" (good): one who is easy with food. In ancient Greek literature, this word sometimes translates Hebrew that speaks of a painful or difficult situation.
G1422.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 10:24. Jesus uses it to express the extreme difficulty for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. The meaning has shifted from the context of meals to that of obstacles or trials: it is something hard to accomplish, requiring a profound transformation. The context shows that Jesus is not speaking of physical impossibility, but of spiritual difficulty: one must renounce reliance on riches to trust in God.
G1422.portee: This word helps the reader to measure the importance of what Jesus teaches: entering the kingdom of God is not an easy endeavor if one remains attached to material wealth. It reminds us that true conversion requires effort and a real inner change. Jesus does not say it is impossible — the following verse emphasizes that nothing is impossible with God — but it calls to take seriously the difficulty of the path to him.

sens: With difficulty, effort, struggling to accomplish something
Almost impossible, very arduous
G1423.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of doing something with a lot of pain and difficulty, as if one must overcome an obstacle. In Matthew 19:23, Jesus says that a rich person will enter the kingdom of heaven "with difficulty": the image is one of struggle, of a painful effort to be made.
2. At its limit, the word emphasizes a near impossibility, so arduous is the task. In Mark 10:23 and Luke 18:24, when Jesus states how "difficult" it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God, he highlights the enormous obstacle that wealth represents — not just a simple hindrance, but a barrier that requires superhuman effort to overcome.
G1423.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "bad" or "difficult" (du-: bad, and the root -skol-: pain, difficulty). It is the adverb formed from the adjective "difficult," very close to it. This root literally evokes the idea of something that is wrong, that is done poorly, hence the notion of pain and labor.
G1423.emploi: This word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the first three Gospels, and always in the same context: the difficulty for the rich to enter the kingdom of God. Matthew translates it as "with difficulty" (an adverb that emphasizes the process, the painful action), while Mark and Luke use "difficult" (the adjective, emphasizing the state of affairs). This choice of vocabulary shows that the three Evangelists want to highlight not a categorical prohibition, but a significant obstacle: it is not "impossible," it is "terribly difficult."
G1423.portee: This word reveals Jesus' crucial teaching on material wealth: it is a formidable spiritual obstacle. Not that it is a sin in itself, but it creates a dependence and attachment that make it extremely difficult to abandon oneself and to trust fully in God. For today's Christian, this word invites examination of where their true trust lies and not to underestimate the grip that material possessions can have on the heart.

sens: The setting sun, its decline toward the horizon
The direction where the sun sets, the west side
The cardinal point opposite to the east
G1424.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the moment when the sun disappears on the horizon — its setting. In Luke 12:54, Jesus speaks of a cloud that "rises in the west," meaning the place where the sun descends and disappears.
2. By extension, it signifies the region or direction from which this sunset comes: the west. This is the dominant meaning in the Gospels and Revelation. Matthew 8:11 and Luke 13:29 speak of people coming "from the east and the west" to enter the kingdom of God — two opposite cardinal points, symbolizing all horizons.
3. In Revelation 21:13, the west simply designates one of the four orientations of the heavenly Jerusalem, with its three gates, just like the north, south, and east.
G1424.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to go" or "to set." It is related to δύνω ("to set," referring to the sun) and to δύσις (another word for the setting or the west). In Hebrew, the word for west can be עֲרָבָה ("west") or בּוֹא ("entry" of the day, hence its decline). The basic image is therefore that of the sun that "descends" or "enters" below the horizon.
G1424.emploi: The word δυσμή appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the singular in the Segond translations. It is used in the Gospels (Matthew, Luke) and in Revelation, never in the Epistles. It consistently designates a geographical or cosmic direction. In Matthew 24:27, the lightning that shines "from the east to the west" illustrates the immediacy and universal visibility of Christ's coming — the west represents the end of the visible world. In eschatological passages (Matthew 8:11; Luke 13:29; Revelation 21:13), the west opposes the east and symbolizes the extent of the world from which the elect are gathered or toward which the new Jerusalem opens its gates.
G1424.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Gospel is intended for all peoples, coming from all horizons. The opposition "east and west" in Jesus' words means: from the rising to the setting, from everywhere. It is a biblical way of saying "from all over the earth" and affirming the universality of salvation. It also roots faith in the concrete reality of the world — God speaks in terms we understand, showing us the sun rising and setting.

sens: That is complex, obscure, and requires intellectual effort to grasp
That lends itself to confusion or misinterpretation
G1425.detail:
1. This word designates what is obscure or complicated to grasp mentally. In 2 Peter 3:16, the apostle speaks of the "difficult points to understand" in Paul's letters: these passages have a deep meaning or a complex formulation that requires reflection and discernment to be well understood. The image is one of a thought that does not immediately present itself to the mind but requires work.
2. By extension, the word also highlights the risk of misunderstanding: precisely because these passages are difficult, ignorant and unstable people distort their meaning to their own ruin. Thus, it is a word that evokes not only intrinsic difficulty but also the vulnerability of one who cannot interpret well.
G1425.origine: The word is composed of the prefix δυσ- (dus-, bad, difficult) and the root νοη- (noē-, which thinks, which understands), derived from the verb νοέω (noéō, to understand, to grasp intellectually). This root νοη- expresses intelligence and intellectual perception. The prefix δυσ- thus makes it the opposite: that which is not easily understood. It is the late Greek that creates this adjective to express a twisted or muddled thought.
G1425.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 3:16. The apostle Peter defends Paul there by acknowledging that some passages of his letters are indeed difficult to understand. But instead of justifying false interpretations, Peter asserts that the difficulty is one more reason to approach these texts with humility and respect for other Scriptures. The context shows that the difficulty of understanding does not excuse the willful distortion of the message: those who twist the meaning do so "to their own ruin."
G1425.portee: This passage reminds the Christian reader that some biblical teachings require discernment and spiritual maturity. Difficulty is not a weakness of the text, but an invitation to seek seriously. It also warns that ignorance and superficial attachment make one vulnerable to false interpretations. This encourages the believer to deepen their faith rather than settle for quick readings.

sens: malicious words spoken against someone
harm to the honor and reputation of a person
public discredit or contempt
G1426.detail:
1. The word δυσφημία primarily refers to malicious words, harmful statements made against someone to belittle them — commonly known as speaking ill of someone, slandering, or defaming.
2. By extension, it refers to the effect of these words: harm to honor, a wound to a person's reputation. In 2 Corinthians 6:8, Paul speaks of being in the midst of "bad reputation": people speak ill of him, say bad things, and this deteriorates his public image.
3. It also refers to discredit, contempt, disgrace — the negative judgment of the public that unfolds publicly. One who suffers from a "bad reputation" is regarded with disdain, suspicion, or dishonor.
G1426.origine: The Greek word is composed of "dus" (bad, difficult) and "phēmē" (word, fame). At its core is the image of a word that deteriorates good fame. The exact opposite is "euphēmia" — eulogy, good reputation. This family of words in Greek describes how words shape reputation, for better or for worse.
G1426.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:8. Paul describes his apostleship as traversing opposites: glory and disgrace, "bad reputation" and good reputation. He accepts being regarded as an impostor despite his truthfulness. This context shows that Paul suffers from "bad reputation" — public discredit — as part of the cost of his obedience, without it reflecting the reality of who he is.
G1426.portee: This word reminds us that reputation and public words are powerful realities. But it also teaches us, through Paul's example, that our true worth before God does not depend on the reputation we have in the eyes of the world. One who proclaims the Gospel may suffer insults and discredit without their faithfulness being affected.

sens: The number 12
The twelve apostles chosen by Jesus
A period of twelve years or twelve days
A quantity of twelve elements or people
G1427.detail:
1. The number twelve simply refers to the numeral 12, used for counting or measuring: "a woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years" (Luke 8:43) or "twelve thousand sealed" from each tribe (Revelation 7:5).
2. "The twelve" becomes a specific title for the apostles that Jesus chose. Jesus "called the twelve" to send them out to preach (Mark 9:35); "Judas, one of the twelve" betrayed him (Matthew 26:47); Jesus said: "Is it not I who chose you, the twelve?" (John 6:70).
3. A duration or interval of twelve units of time: the woman with the flow of blood suffered "for twelve years," and the young Jesus fulfilled the law's requirements at "twelve years" (Luke 2:42).
4. A precise quantity of twelve objects or people: the leftovers of the loaves, gathered in "twelve baskets" (Mark 6:43), or the "twelve tribes of Israel" promised for future judgment (Luke 22:30).
G1427.origine: The Greek word δώδεκα (dôdeka) is an unalterable numeral that comes from ancient Greek. It is composed of δύο (dyo, "two") and δέκα (déka, "ten"), literally "two-ten." This number has a strong symbolic charge in the Hebrew Bible: the twelve tribes of Israel, the twelve stones of the sanctuary, reflect the order and completeness of God's people.
G1427.emploi: The word "twelve" appears 62 times in the New Testament. It is first used simply for counting or measuring: ages, years, sums of money, quantities of food. But it takes on special theological significance when it designates "the twelve apostles" or "the twelve" — this group that Jesus constituted. The Gospels emphasize the calling of the twelve (Mark 3:14: "he called twelve"), their missions (Mark 6:7), their progressive understanding (Mark 4:10), and the betrayal of one of them (Matthew 26:47, John 6:70). Revelation also uses "twelve" to evoke the eternal structures of divine reign: the twelve tribes, the twelve gates, and the twelve foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12-14).
G1427.portee: The number twelve, in its systematic use, reminds readers that Jesus chose a limited and defined group to be his witnesses. This choice is deliberate and significant: it refers to Israel's twelve tribes and announces that the Church is the new Israel. The presence and actions of "the twelve" structure all of Jesus' ministry and the birth of the Church: they embody the transmission of apostolic authority.

sens: the ordinal number 12, which comes after the eleventh
rank or position occupying the twelfth order in a series
G1428.detail:
1. The word designates the ordinal number twelve, the one that follows the eleventh in an order or enumeration. In Revelation 21:20, it qualifies the twelfth precious stone that adorns the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem: the amethyst, thus inscribing this number in a succession of precious materials meant to adorn the holy city.
2. More generally, the word situates something in the twelfth place, marking its rank in an ordered set. It is a tool for counting and classifying, essential when enumerating a series and designating each step by its order number.
G1428.origine: The Greek word derives from "dōdeka" (twelve) augmented by the ordinal suffix "-tos" which transforms a cardinal number into an ordinal — the same suffix as in French in "deuxième" or "cinquième." This formation is common in Greek: "tris" (three) becomes "tritos" (third), "tessares" (four) becomes "tetartos" (fourth). The number 12 holds major symbolic importance in the Bible: the 12 tribes of Israel, the 12 apostles of Jesus, the 12 gates and 12 foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem.
G1428.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:20, where John enumerates the twelve precious stones that form the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem. It appears in an ordered list ("the first... the second..."), where each stone occupies a specific place. The use of the ordinal number emphasizes that each foundation has its particular value in the glorious edifice that God is preparing. It is a language of meticulous description and harmony: nothing is left to chance, each element has its rank.
G1428.portee: The twelfth rank, in this apocalyptic vision, reminds the reader that the 12 stones correspond to the 12 apostles and the 12 tribes: God thus completes the work of covenant that the Old Testament began. This enumerative detail nourishes the confidence that every element of Christian life, from the most visible to the most hidden, occupies a place intended by the Lord in his plan of redemption.

sens: The entirety of the twelve tribes of Israel, God's chosen people
G1429.detail: 1. The expression "twelve tribes" refers to the twelve divisions of the people of Israel, based on the twelve sons of Jacob. It is a term that encompasses all of Israel in its totality and unity. In Acts 26:7, Paul speaks of the eschatological hope towards which "these twelve tribes aspire": it is the messianic promise and the resurrection of the dead, the very heart of Israel's expectation.
G1429.origine: The Greek word δωδεκάφυλος (dōdekaphulos) is composed of δώδεκα (dōdeka, "twelve") and φυλή (phylē, "tribe"). It simply translates the Hebrew idea of the people of Israel divided into twelve genealogical branches, tracing back to the twelve sons of Jacob-Israel. This number twelve holds central theological importance: it symbolizes the fullness and completeness of God's people.
G1429.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:7, during Paul's defense speech before King Agrippa. Paul evokes the common messianic hope of all the tribes of Israel, that which all the faithful "aspire" continually in the service of God. This context shows that the expression does not simply describe an administrative or geographical division, but the entirety of the people called to live in expectation of the divine promise.
G1429.portee: For a Christian reader, this mention of the twelve tribes reminds us that the Church does not annul the promises made to Israel, but is part of their fulfillment. The aspiration that Paul speaks of is also that of the believer: the resurrection and eternal life promised. It is an invitation to grasp that our hope rests on these same divine promises that have animated God's people throughout the ages.

sens: The top of a house, covered with tiles or flat
A public and accessible place from which to shout or make something known
G1430.detail:
1. The roof is the upper part of a house, the part that covers it. In Israel and the Mediterranean, roofs are generally flat, forming a terrace where one can walk and work. This is where the friends of the paralytic lower him down in Luke 5:19, "they went up on the roof," digging through the roofing to let him down.
2. The roof also becomes a biblical image of what is public, visible, proclaimed to the world. Jesus says in Matthew 10:27: "What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; what is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the roofs," meaning: what you learn in secret must be proclaimed loudly. The roof is the place where all can see and hear.
G1430.origine: The Greek word δῶμα comes from the root δέμω which means "to build, to construct." It first designates the entire dwelling, then more specifically its upper part, the roof. In classical Athenian Greek, other terms were preferred; δῶμα is a word from poets and later texts, appearing in the Greek translation of the Old Testament to render the Hebrew גָּג (gag), the roof, particularly in passages where one goes up on the roof to pray or act.
G1430.emploi: The word roof appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in the synoptic gospels. It is used concretely to describe actions: in Luke 5:19, men go up on the roof to lower a sick person; in Acts 10:9, Peter goes up on the roof to pray. It is also used to express the idea of public proclamation: Jesus uses it in Matthew 10:27 and Luke 12:3 to invite his disciples to announce the Gospel without fear. Finally, during the destruction of Jerusalem, Jesus warns in Matthew 24:17 and Mark 13:15 those who will be on the roof to flee without going down — the roof becomes a place of urgent escape, where one must act quickly.
G1430.portee: The roof teaches the believer that nothing should remain hidden from the truth received from the Lord: it is meant to be proclaimed in broad daylight. This word also reminds that the disciple does not fear the judgment of men, but accepts that his faith be known to all. Finally, in times of crisis, the roof is a symbol of spiritual urgency: one must quickly choose between saving one's life and saving one's possessions.

sens: A present offered freely, without expectation of return
The gift of the Holy Spirit given to believers
Divine grace or favor granted freely
A present or benefit received for free
G1431.detail:
1. The word δωρεά designates a gift given to someone, not out of obligation or exchange, but out of pure kindness. This is what Jesus explains to the Samaritan woman: the "gift of God" is the living water he offers without asking for any payment in return (John 4:10). The word emphasizes the complete absence of any counter-gift.

2. In Acts, the term often refers to the gift of the Holy Spirit, this supernatural gift that God pours out on believers at the moment of their conversion or spiritual filling (Acts 2:38, 10:45). Peter categorically refuses Simon the Magician's attempt to buy this gift: "May your money perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!" (Acts 8:20).

3. Paul uses the word to speak of God's gifts in general: grace itself (Romans 5:15, Ephesians 3:7), the righteousness offered freely (Romans 5:17), or the gifts of Christ given to the Church (Ephesians 4:7). Each time, the idea is one of God's limitless generosity.

4. In Hebrews 6:4, we read: "those who have been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift": here, the gift includes all the spiritual blessings received from God, enlightenment and the experience of salvation.
G1431.origine: The word δωρεά comes from the verb δίδωμι, which means "to give." It specifically designates a free gift, without commercial exchange. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it primarily translates the Hebrew word חִנָּם (ḥinnâm), which means "for free" or "for nothing." This root emphasizes one of the most beautiful realities of the biblical message: God's gifts cannot be bought, earned, they are received with gratitude.
G1431.emploi: The word δωρεά appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and Paul's epistles. In Acts (2:38, 8:20, 10:45, 11:17), it almost always designates the gift of the Holy Spirit, this fundamental gift given to all who believe in Jesus. In Paul, the term expands: he speaks of the gift of grace (Romans 5:15), the gift of righteousness (Romans 5:17), the gift of God manifested in Christ. In Ephesians, Paul mentions the gifts of Christ distributed in the Church (4:7). In Hebrews 6:4, the term encompasses all the illuminations and spiritual experiences granted by God. In every use, the word emphasizes the free and unmerited nature of God's gift.
G1431.portee: This word reminds Christians of a fundamental truth: salvation, the Holy Spirit, grace, righteousness before God — all of this cannot be bought, conquered, or earned. They are pure gifts of God's goodness. When reading δωρεά, the reader understands that their relationship with God does not rest on a system of exchange or performance, but on the grateful reception of an inexhaustible generosity. This frees from guilt and calls for gratitude.

sens: Without payment, without return, offered freely
Offered as a gift, without having earned it
In vain, without result, uselessly
G1432.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an action done without asking for payment: it is done freely, given without the recipient having to pay. Jesus sends his disciples saying: "Freely you have received; freely give" (Matthew 10:8) — they have received the power to heal without paying for it, and they must pass it on in the same way.
2. The word also applies to what is received as a pure gift, a grace, without having earned or purchased it. Humans "are justified freely by his grace" (Romans 3:24): forgiveness and righteousness come from God as a pure gift, not as a reward earned.
3. In some passages, the word takes the opposite meaning: an action done freely can also be a vain action, which produces nothing. In Galatians 2:21, renouncing the grace of Christ would make his death useless — it would have been poured out "in vain," freely and without effect.
G1432.origine: The word δωρεάν (dōrean) comes from δωρεά (dōrea), which means "gift" or "present." It is an accusative used as an adverb, describing the action in the form of a gift. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew חִנָּם (hinnam), which means "without reason, freely." The root δίδωμι means "to give," which shows that the word is related to the idea of generosity.
G1432.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, almost always in the positive sense of an action offered without payment. Jesus uses it for teaching and miracles: the disciples must proclaim the Gospel freely (Matthew 10:8, 2 Corinthians 11:7). Paul emphasizes that he worked without being supported, eating his bread "freely," meaning without receiving it as a gift from others (2 Thessalonians 3:8). The word also characterizes God's action: justification is given freely (Romans 3:24), and the water of life is offered freely to anyone who is thirsty (Revelation 21:6, 22:17). Only once, in Galatians 2:21, does the word take the meaning of "in vain" or "uselessly."
G1432.portee: This word reminds the believer that salvation, righteousness, and forgiveness are pure gifts from God, not commodities to be bought or rewards to be earned. It also invites the Church to imitate this model: those who have received freely must give freely. For Paul, this is a principle of dignity and Christian freedom: the servant of Christ should not be a burden, and the Gospel should never be turned into commerce.

sens: To hand something over to someone, to entrust it to them
To grant, bestow, to present something
G1433.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of physically handing something over to someone. Mark 15:45 provides a concrete example: Pilate "gave the body to Joseph," meaning he handed it over for burial. It is an act of direct transmission, from hand to hand or from an authority to a person.

2. In a figurative sense, the verb means to grant, bestow, to give something of value, often what comes from God. In 2 Peter 1:4, divine promises are "given" to us — God generously grants them to transform us internally and make us partakers of His divine nature.
G1433.origine: The verb δωρέω comes from δῶρον (doron), which means "gift" or "present." This is why it carries the idea of generosity and gratuity: to give is to make a present. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates נָתַן (natan), the classical Hebrew verb for "to give," showing that in the Bible, giving is a fundamental gesture, whether human or divine.
G1433.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always with a nuance of solemnity or importance. In Mark 15:45, it is Pilate who "gives" the body of Jesus to Joseph of Arimathea, marking an official and decisive act. In 2 Peter 1:3-4, Paul uses this verb to express how God "gives" us His precious promises — a free and majestic divine gift. The verb thus emphasizes the sense of "officially handing over" or "generously granting," rather than a simple transfer of possession.
G1433.portee: This word reminds us that God is the one who "gives" generously and freely. When the Bible speaks of God "giving" us His promises, His grace, or His divine nature, it teaches us that what transforms us does not come from our efforts, but from the generous heart of the Father. It is an invitation to receive with gratitude and to recognize all good as coming from God.

sens: a present offered freely, without expectation of return
favor granted by grace
divine benefit
G1434.detail:
1. A free gift is a present received without having earned or purchased it: it is God who offers it freely. In Romans 5:16, Paul contrasts it with judgment: while Adam's sin brought condemnation for all, the free gift of God brings justification — this unmerited gift of forgiveness.
2. This word also designates a favor granted out of pure kindness, without obligation. James 1:17 speaks of "every good and perfect gift" that comes down from the Father of lights: it refers to all the goods that God grants us simply because He is good, without us having done anything to deserve them.
3. The free gift is particularly a divine benefit — something that comes solely from God and does not depend on our efforts or merits.
G1434.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to give," and the suffix -μα indicates the result of the action: that which is given. The Greek verb δωρέω (to give) is related to δῶρον (present, gift). This term emphasizes the gratuity of the gift — it is not a wage earned, but a favor freely granted.
G1434.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Romans 5:16, Paul uses it in his argument about salvation: the free gift of God erases offenses and brings justification, unlike the judgment that leads to death. In James 1:17, it designates divine blessings in general — wisdom, strength, providence — that the heavenly Father dispenses without us having anything to give in return. These two uses emphasize that divine generosity is never a due: it is pure grace.
G1434.portee: This word helps the believer understand the heart of the Gospel: salvation is not a reward that we could earn, but a gift that God gives us out of pure love. It also invites us to recognize every blessing — great or small — as an unmerited favor from the Father, which should transform our gratitude and trust in Him.

sens: a present offered to someone as a sign of honor or affection
an offering brought to God at the temple, a material sacrifice
that which is granted freely, without merit from the recipient
G1435.detail:
1. A gift is primarily a concrete present offered to someone to honor them or to please them. The Magi brought gifts to the child Jesus: gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matthew 2:11). It is a precious object given out of affection or respect.
2. In the temple worship, a gift is a religious offering: one brings a sacrifice, a consecrated object, to God. Jesus reminds us that before presenting one's offering at the altar, one must reconcile with their brother (Matthew 5:24). This shows that a material gift to God has value only if the heart is pure.
3. In a spiritual sense, the gift is what one receives without having earned it, out of pure generosity. The grace of salvation is a gift from God: we are saved by faith, "and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God" (Ephesians 2:8). Here, it is God who gives, and man can only receive.
G1435.origine: The word comes from the verb "to give" (δίδωμι, didōmi). It designates the act of giving seen from the perspective of what is given: the gift, the present. In Hebrew, δῶρον primarily translates קׇרְבָּן (qorban), which means "that which approaches" — the offering brought near to God at the temple. This is why the biblical gift is never neutral: it engages the giver and establishes a relationship with the receiver.
G1435.emploi: The word δῶρον appears 17 times in the New Testament. It first designates ordinary presents, such as the gifts of the Magi (Matthew 2:11). But its primary use is religious: it refers to offerings brought to the temple, especially in the Gospel of Matthew and the Letter to the Hebrews. Matthew uses it to show how Jesus criticizes the abuse of offerings: religious leaders teach that a gift to God exempts one from honoring their parents (Matthew 15:5, 23:18-19). Hebrews uses it to describe the sacrifices of the old covenant (Hebrews 5:1, 8:3-4, 9:9, 11:4). Finally, Ephesians 2:8 applies it to grace itself, the salvific gift of God that does not depend on our works.
G1435.portee: This word reminds us that every good received comes from God and that no human work can merit it. The offerings at the temple engaged the people to recognize God's lordship, but Jesus shows that God prefers a pure heart to a material gift. For the Christian, meditating on the divine gift invites gratitude towards the Lord and generosity towards others, knowing that what we have, we have received.

sens: Exclamation of astonishment or indignation, of fear
Expression of surprise in the face of an unexpected intervention
Mark of trouble and protest
G1436.detail:
1. This exclamation conveys the raw emotion of a character who did not expect what is happening: surprise, fear, or sudden protest. In Luke 4:34, the demon who recognizes Jesus exclaims, "Ah! What do we have to do with you?", thus expressing its panic and protest in the face of this threatening encounter.
2. It marks the moment when something unexpected or undesirable disturbs: it is the exclamation of one who feels confronted by an intrusion, a threat, or an event that disturbs them. The demon, in Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34, uses it to express its concern in the presence of Jesus' power, which puts it in danger.
G1436.origine: The interjection ἔα is a natural cry in classical Greek, especially in poetry, to express raw emotion. It does not have a complex etymology: it is simply the phonetic expression of an affective reaction. It is formed like a primitive cry, similar to the natural interjections of spoken language.
G1436.emploi: The word appears twice, both in the parallel account of a demonic possession (Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34), where an unclean spirit possessing a man addresses Jesus.
