The exclamation "Ah!" reveals the fear and indignation of the demon in the presence of the Messiah. It is never used by ordinary human characters, but only by this supernatural creature that feels threatened. The usage shows how the interjection conveys an intense and immediate emotional reaction.
G1436.portee: This exclamation reveals that evil spirits experience genuine fear in the face of Jesus and His authority: even before He speaks, the mere contact with His presence causes them to panic. For the Christian reader, it testifies to the power and reality of Jesus' spiritual authority, feared even by dark powers. It also shows us that the confrontation with Christ is not neutral: it provokes a reaction, either of faith or of fear and resistance.

sens: particle that introduces a supposed possible condition
serves to express a hypothesis or supposition
introduces a consequence that depends on a condition
marks an alternative or a question with doubt
G1437.detail:
1. ἐάν poses a condition: it presents something as "possibly occurring under certain circumstances," without asserting that it is certain. For example, in Matthew 4:9, the devil says to Jesus, "If you fall down and worship me, I will give you all these things." The prostration is the supposed condition.
2. It expresses a hypothesis that the speaker does not consider certain: "If anyone tells you, 'Look, here is the Christ...' do not believe it" (Matthew 24:23). The text contemplates a possibility.
3. It links a condition to its consequences: in 1 Corinthians 8:8, "if we eat food, we gain nothing; if we do not eat, we lose nothing." Each branch of the condition has its effect.
4. It can also mark a question that expresses doubt or hypothesis: "If he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion?" (Luke 11:12). The interrogative form emphasizes the absurd impossibility.
G1437.origine: ἐάν is the contraction of two Greek particles: εἰ ("if") and ἄν (the modal particle that makes an action conditional or virtual). It thus comes from the fusion of these two words to mean "if ever" or "if by chance." This contraction gradually became established, and ἐάν became the standard form in New Testament Greek to express a condition that is not certain. It is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew formulas with אִם ("if").
G1437.emploi: ἐάν is the most common word in the New Testament to introduce a condition (319 occurrences). It appears in all the gospels and epistles, especially in Matthew and John. It usually accompanies the present or aorist subjunctive, which marks uncertainty or supposability. For example, in Matthew 5:19, "whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments..." (where the aorist subjunctive expresses a possible future action). Sometimes it combines with other particles: "if... and" (Galatians 6:1), "if... not" (Matthew 6:15), or "either... or" (Romans 14:8). It can even introduce a condition in the future or present indicative, especially in the later Greek of the New Testament (Acts 7:7, 1 Thessalonians 3:8). Its usage reflects the New Testament's concern: to present the conditions of salvation, moral consequences, and divine promises in terms of real possibility and human freedom.
G1437.portee: This word reveals the very structure of the biblical message: God does not force anyone, He proposes conditions and consequences. "If you believe...", "if you keep...", "if you love...": God's promises depend on our response. This reminds the Christian reader that they have a responsibility in their relationship with God and that blessings are not automatic, but are linked to our choice to follow Him.

sens: reflexive pronoun of the 3rd person: himself, herself, oneself
G1438.detail: 1. This word is a reflexive pronoun: it refers to the person performing the action, to express that they act upon themselves or think something. For example, when Mark 2:8 reports that Jesus "knew in Himself" what the scribes were thinking, the pronoun refers to Jesus Himself. Or in Matthew 3:9, John the Baptist says to the Pharisees: "do not presume to say to yourselves," meaning in your own mind. 2. This same word can also express a relationship between several people: "between them," "one another" (reciprocal sense). For example, in Mark 14:4, some "expressed their indignation among themselves," each with the others. 3. It can reinforce a possessive: "his own clothes," "his own life." For example, in Luke 9:60, when Jesus says, "let the dead bury their own dead," He emphasizes that each must take care of what concerns them. 4. Used with certain prepositions, it takes on particular nuances: "of oneself" (Luke 21:30: "you know it of yourselves"), "in oneself" (Mark 6:51: "in Himself"), "at home" (1 Corinthians 16:2: "at his home").
G1438.origine: This pronoun comes from ancient Greek. It is mainly used to fulfill the function of a reflexive in the 3rd person ("him," "her," "oneself"), where French would use "se" or a possessive adjective. In Hebrew, the idea is often rendered by a suffix pronoun attached to the verb or noun (for example, "he kept himself"). It is a grammatical tool that Greek uses extensively to clarify who acts and who is affected by the action.
G1438.emploi: This pronoun appears more than 300 times in the New Testament, used in all the Gospels and the letters of Paul. It is mainly used in three contexts: first to express that a person acts upon themselves or thinks to themselves (Matthew 3:9, Mark 2:8, Luke 12:57); then to say "between them" or "one another" when speaking of several (Mark 14:4, Ephesians 5:19); finally to reinforce a possessive, especially when wanting to emphasize the personal nature of something (Luke 9:60). The context and the prepositions that accompany the word (of, in, at, towards, beside) slightly change its meaning.
G1438.portee: Understanding this pronoun helps to see how much the Bible is concerned with inner struggle, hidden thoughts, and personal choices. When it says that someone "thought to themselves" or "said to themselves," it shows that God probes hearts and secret intentions. It is also a reminder that each person is responsible for themselves: everyone must know themselves, judge themselves, and keep themselves. This intimacy of biblical language speaks to today's reader on their own faith journey.

sens: To allow something to happen, not to prevent it
To leave a person alone, to stop imposing something on them
To abandon, to forsake something or someone
G1439.detail:
1. To permit or authorize an action: this means not intervening to prevent it. Jesus "did not allow" the demons to speak (Luke 4:41) — he could have let them cry out, but he restrained them. God "allowed" the ancient nations to follow their own ways (Acts 14:16) — he did not prevent them, he respected their freedom.
2. To leave someone alone, to stop an action towards them: Jesus says "Let it be, stop!" when the soldiers strike (Luke 22:51) — he asks that the violence cease. It is to command someone to stop continuing what they were doing.
3. To abandon or set aside something: the soldiers "let" the horsemen pursue alone (Acts 23:32) — they separate from them. The sailors "let go" the anchors (Acts 27:40) — they abandon them as they depart.
G1439.origine: The verb ἐάω comes from a root expressing the idea of yielding, of not resisting. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates the verb רפה (raphah) in the sense of "to release, to let go." The word belongs to the family of action or inaction verbs: to let is to choose not to act, to permit instead of commanding.
G1439.emploi: This verb appears eleven times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It describes Jesus preventing demons from speaking (Luke 4:41), ordering that violence be stopped (Luke 22:51), or the master who could have "let" his house be burglarized if he had not been vigilant (Matthew 24:43). In Acts, it is used for the action of the Spirit who "did not allow" the apostles to go to Bithynia (Acts 16:7), or for practical gestures of abandoning things: leaving the horsemen, leaving the ship's anchors. The meaning oscillates between "to allow" and "to abandon," depending on the context and what follows the verb.
G1439.portee: This word reminds us that power also resides in the choice not to act: to permit is an act. For the reader, it invites reflection on what God "allows" to happen — not out of indifference, but sometimes to respect human freedom, sometimes to discipline. It is also a call to recognize when the Spirit "allows" or "forbids" a path: listening to this guidance is to embrace God's will.

sens: The number 70
A group of seventy people or things
G1440.detail:
1. This word simply denotes the number 70. It is a composite number formed on the base 7 (seven), with the suffix -konta indicating tens. In the Bible, 70 often appears as a symbolic number: the seventy disciples sent by Jesus in Luke 10:1, or seventy-seven people from Jacob's family in Acts 7:14.
2. The word is used to count concrete people or things: the seventy horsemen that the tribune sends to escort Paul to Caesarea (Acts 23:23), or the two hundred seventy-six souls on board the ship in Acts 27:37. It is a factual number, used for enumeration or counting.
G1440.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "hepta" (seven) and the suffix "-konta" (which means ten times). This suffix "-konta" is used to form all the numbers from 20 to 90 in ancient Greek: 20 (eikosi), 30 (triakonta), 40 (tessarakonta), 50 (pentekonta), 60 (hexekonta), 70, 80 (ogdoekonta), 90 (enenekonta). It is a regular grammatical process for counting tens in Greek.
G1440.emploi: The number 70 appears 5 times in the provided passages, all in the New Testament. In Luke, it refers to the disciples sent on mission: 70 disciples at the start (Luke 10:1) who return filled with joy after experiencing the power of Jesus' name (Luke 10:17). In Acts, the number becomes descriptive and factual: 75 people from Jacob's kin according to tradition (Acts 7:14), 70 horsemen among Paul's military escort (Acts 23:23), and 276 people in total on the ship heading to Rome (Acts 27:37). The word never changes meaning; it is the context that varies between symbolic use and literal counting.
G1440.portee: The number 70, while here a simple figure, reminds the reader that Jesus does not send out one apostle or two, but creates a collective movement: he multiplies his workers for the harvest of the Kingdom. When these seventy return in Luke 10:17, they testify that the power of Jesus operates through his ordinary disciples. This number also evokes abundance and fullness, images that run throughout biblical preaching.

sens: The number seventy repeated, that is, a very large and indefinite number of times
G1441.detail: 1. The adverb literally means "seventy times." In Matthew 18:22, Jesus uses it to say that forgiveness must be granted "seventy times seven times," meaning an incalculable number of times, without limit or count. It is not exact arithmetic, but a way of saying that forgiveness must be endless: Peter had suggested forgiving seven times, a number already generous according to Jewish custom, and Jesus raises it to a limit that only the heart can measure.
G1441.origine: The Greek word comes from the number seventy (ἑβδομήκοντα, "hebdomékonta") and the suffix -άκις which repeats this number: literally "seventy-times." In Hebrew, Genesis 4:24 uses the same type of expression, where Lamech promises vengeance "seventy-seven times" — a number symbolizing excess and infinity. The Greek thus translates the biblical image of infinity by the repetition of a large number.
G1441.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 18:22. Jesus responds to Peter who asks if he should forgive up to seven times: "No, not seven times, but seventy times seven times." This response pushes any limit on forgiveness away. The expression is not a mathematical formula to calculate, but a biblical hyperbole, an intentional exaggeration to show that the disciple's forgiveness must imitate God's forgiveness — without measure or end.
G1441.portee: This passage calls the Christian to go beyond vengeance and resentment, not by tolerating evil, but by opening their heart to unrestricted forgiveness. Seventy times seven reminds us that divine grace itself has no limits. For one who has received God's infinite forgiveness in Christ, refusing forgiveness to a brother is an unbearable contradiction.

sens: Which comes in seventh position in a series or enumeration
Which marks the seventh hour of the day
Which designates the day of rest instituted by God in Creation
G1442.detail:
1. The word designates what occupies the seventh place in an order or succession. In Revelation, we speak of the seventh seal, the seventh angel, the seventh thunder: each comes after six others, forming a complete series. In Jude 1:14, Enoch is the seventh from Adam, which means there are six generations before him.

2. In John 4:52, the seventh hour refers to a specific moment of the day: it is around one o'clock in the afternoon (one hour in modern time). The Jews counted the hours of the day from sunrise, so the seventh hour marked a specific moment of the day.

3. In Hebrews 4:4, the seventh day is the day when God rested after creation — this day symbolizes divine rest and becomes a figure of the eternal rest promised to believers. It is a particular day, blessed and sanctified, which recalls the order intended by God from the beginning.
G1442.origine: The word comes from the Greek heptas (ἑπτὰ), which means "seven." In Greek, the suffix -mos is added to the number to form the ordinal adjective: seventh. The Greek hebdomos regularly translates the Hebrew shebii (שְׁבִיעִי) in the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew word literally meaning "the one who comes seventh." This notion of the seventh day goes back to the Creation account in Genesis, where God rests on the seventh day and blesses it.
G1442.emploi: The word appears about ten times, especially in Revelation, where it structures the unfolding of the visions: the seven seals, the seven angels, the seven trumpets. It also designates a moment of the day in John 4:52 (the seventh hour of the day). In Hebrews 4:4, it evokes the rest of the seventh day instituted by God at Creation, a rest that the author sees as the ultimate fulfillment for the people of God. In Jude 1:14, it genealogically situates Enoch. The number seven holds theological significance in the Bible: it symbolizes fullness, completion, and holiness, which gives the seventh a particular spiritual weight in the apocalyptic context.
G1442.portee: The seventh day reminds us that rest is not a luxury, but a gift from God inscribed in His creation. For the believer, it speaks of the true rest found in Jesus Christ, a rest of faith in which one ceases to justify oneself by works. In Revelation, the seventh seals and angels mark the approach of divine fulfillment, inviting the reader to hold on knowing that history is moving towards God's final victory.

sens: Distant ancestor of Jesus, in the genealogy of Luke
G1443.detail: Eber is a figure from the Old Testament mentioned in the genealogy that traces back from Jesus to Adam (Luke 3:35). He is the son of Sala and the father of Peleg. This name also appears in Genesis 10:24 in the Hebrew text, where he is listed among the descendants of Shem after the Flood. His name means "the one who passes" or "the one from the other side," an allusion to those who crossed or lived on the other side of the Euphrates River. Luke includes him in his genealogy to show that Jesus descends from an unbroken lineage going back to the pre-flood patriarchs.
G1443.origine: The Hebrew name עֵבֶר (Eber) comes from a root meaning "to pass" or "to cross." This name evokes the Hebrews themselves, whose name likely comes from the same family of words, designating those who came "from the other side" (of the river). Eber is a distant ancestor of the people of Israel and of the Hebrew tradition.
G1443.emploi: Eber appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:35, in the complete genealogy that Luke provides of Jesus. This family tree, which traces back from Jesus to Adam, seeks to establish the continuity of the divine promise throughout history. Eber occupies an important place, about ten generations before Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people. His inclusion emphasizes that Jesus is part of the history of salvation from the very beginning.
G1443.portee: The mention of Eber in Luke's genealogy reminds us that Jesus is not an isolated figure, but the culmination of a divine promise that spans millennia. It invites the reader to see in the life of Jesus the fulfillment of what God has prepared since ancient times.

sens: belonging to the Hebrew language and people
concerning Judea and its inhabitants
G1444.detail:
1. This adjective qualifies what is related to the Hebrew language spoken and written in Judea. In the Passion, the inscription on Jesus' cross was written in three languages: Hebrew (the language of the local people), Latin (the language of Rome), and Greek (lingua franca), and each was meant to be readable by the different inhabitants of Jerusalem (Luke 23:38).
2. More broadly, "Hebrew" designates what belongs to the Jewish people and their culture, in contrast to Greek or Roman.
G1444.origine: The Greek word "hebraikos" comes from the name of the Hebrews themselves, whose etymology remains debated but originally referred to the people established in the Holy Land. In Greek, this regularly formed adjective literally means "of the type of Hebrews." It is one of the Greek words used to speak of what pertains to Judea and its Jewish population.
G1444.emploi: This adjective appears only once in the New Testament in Luke 23:38, in the context of the crucifixion of Jesus. Matthew, Mark, and John also mention the inscription on the cross (titulus), but only Luke specifies that it was in three languages. The term "Hebrew" emphasizes that the language of the holy land was present even in the eyes of the Roman occupier, thus affirming the Jewish identity of the place and its King.
G1444.portee: For the believer, this detail reminds us that Jesus was crucified on His own territory, in the presence of witnesses from all backgrounds — and that the message of His kingship was proclaimed in the very language of His ancestors. It is a mark of God's solidarity with His people, even at the moment of judgment.

sens: Jew of Semitic language and culture, speaking Aramaic or Hebrew rather than Greek
Israelite of the Old Testament, in contrast with foreign peoples
G1445.detail:
1. In the New Testament, a Hebrew is a Jew who has retained the Semitic language and customs of his ancestors — Aramaic or Hebrew — rather than adopting the Greek language and culture as the Hellenists did. This is why the apostle Paul can say "Hebrew of Hebrews" (Philippians 3:5), emphasizing his fidelity to ancestral tradition. The term thus designates a cultural and linguistic reality: it is not just a Jew, but a Jew who has chosen to remain attached to his Semitic roots.

2. In the Old Testament, the word designates the Israelites, distinguishing them from surrounding peoples. Abram is called "the Hebrew" when he distinguishes himself from the Canaanites (Genesis 14:13), and the Hebrew midwives are those who deliver the children of Israel, not the Egyptians (Exodus 1:15). It is a term of national and religious identity.
G1445.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic עִבְרַי (ibraya), which is itself related to the root עָבַר (avar: "to pass"). The name "Hebrew" may derive from Eber, an ancestor of Abraham in the biblical genealogy, or evoke the idea of "one who has crossed" (reference to the crossing of the Jordan or the arrival in Canaan). In the ancient Greek Bible, this word often replaces the Hebrew עִבְרִי (ivri) or עֵבֶר. In biblical French, the feminine form "Hébraïque" or the adjective to designate the Hebrew language is also encountered.
G1445.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always to designate a specific Jew, in contrast with the Hellenists — Jews of Greek culture. In Acts 6:1, the Hebrews are distinguished from the Hellenists in the early Church of Jerusalem, particularly in the distribution of aid to widows. Paul in 2 Corinthians 11:22 and Philippians 3:5 boasts of being "Hebrew of Hebrews," affirming that he has not abandoned his Semitic identity despite his Greek education. The word never designates a mere religious belonging to the people of Israel, but always a linguistic and cultural fidelity to ancient traditions.
G1445.portee: This term reminds the believer that faith in Jesus does not erase identity and cultural heritage. The apostle Paul, although he preached to the Greeks, remained proud of his Hebrew roots — a model of fidelity to origins while serving the universal Christ. For us, this invites us to honor the Hebrew and Semitic dimension of our faith, rooted in the Old Testament and the history of Israel.

sens: the language spoken by the Hebrews and Jews of Palestine
the vernacular Aramaic used at the time of the New Testament
the dialect or speech of a region or group
G1446.detail:
1. The word designates the language of the Hebrews, that of the people of God of the Old Testament. When Paul speaks "in the Hebrew language" in Jerusalem (Acts 21:40), he uses this language to be better understood and to honor his Jewish compatriots. It is a deliberate and respectful choice.
2. In the context of the New Testament, this "Hebrew language" is actually Aramaic, the dialect spoken daily by the Jews of Palestine in the first century — not the classical Hebrew of the Old Testament. When the voice of Christ addresses Paul in Aramaic: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 26:14), it uses precisely this popular, immediate, and living speech.
3. The term "dialect" emphasizes that it is a linguistic variant specific to a place or group: the recognizable and authentic way of speaking of the inhabitants of Judea and Galilee.
G1446.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic עִבְרַי (ibrai), which means "Hebrew." In Greek, it takes the feminine form Ἑβραΐς (Hebrais) when referring to the language. The Greeks borrowed this term to designate the language of the people of God. In the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament), the expression "the Hebrew voice" is found to describe a word in this language.
G1446.emploi: The word appears three times in Acts, each time to indicate that Paul or a divine voice is addressing the Jews in their own speech. In Acts 21:40, Paul obtains permission to speak to the crowd in the Hebrew language after his arrest in Jerusalem, which creates attentive silence. In Acts 22:2, the silence deepens when the Jews hear this same language. In Acts 26:14, it is the voice of the risen Lord that addresses Paul in Aramaic, marking him deeply. The word always emphasizes the importance of speaking the mother tongue of the people to reach their heart and mind.
G1446.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Gospel meets people in their own language and culture. Paul does not impose himself in Greek or Latin: he honors his listeners by speaking as they speak. Likewise, the voice of the risen Christ uses familiar Aramaic, showing that God speaks the language of the human heart. It is a lesson in incarnation and missionary humility: divine truth gains power when proclaimed in the living language of a people.

sens: in the Hebrew or Aramaic language
expressed in Hebrew or Aramaic, according to local usages
G1447.detail: 1. The word designates the Hebrew language or, in the context of the New Testament, the Aramaic spoken in Judea — the two Semitic languages of the Jewish people. When the Gospel says that the pool of Bethesda is called "in Hebrew" Bethesda (John 5:2), it indicates that this is the name used by the Jews themselves in their own language, as opposed to Greek or Latin. Similarly, the place of the skull is named "in Hebrew" Golgotha (John 19:17), which literally means "place of the skull" in the language of the land. 2. This word also emphasizes the authenticity and authority of the reported words when they are preserved in the original language. When Mary Magdalene says to Jesus "Rabbouni" "in Hebrew" (John 20:16), this detail highlights the immediacy and personal depth of this exchange — it is the language of the heart, the mother tongue of faith.
G1447.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "Hebraios" (Hebrew, Israelite) formed from the root of the people and language of Hebrews. It is pure Greek that simply describes the Semitic language of the Jews of Palestine. The word appears mainly in the Gospels of John and in Revelation, written for a community in close contact with the realities of Judean terrain.
G1447.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospel of John (5 occurrences) and Revelation (2 occurrences). John uses it to preserve authentic words of Jesus or names of places as they were pronounced in Jerusalem: Bethesda (pool), Gabbatha (the pavement where Pilate sat), Golgotha (the Calvary), Rabbouni (Master), and the cry from the cross. Revelation uses it for Abaddon, the angel of the abyss. This process — reporting the original word in the Semitic language — confers a strength of authenticity and anchors the narrative in the historical reality of first-century Judea.
G1447.portee: This word reminds the reader that the events of Jesus' life took place in Jewish land, in the language of the chosen people. It also preserves the intimacy of key moments: when Mary recognizes the Risen One and calls him "Rabbouni," the evangelist retains this personal word in its original language, as a living testimony. It is an invitation to enter into the concrete faith of the people of Israel and to respect the Jewish roots of the Gospel.

sens: To draw near in space, referring to distance
To arrive, to happen for an event or a time
To become close, imminent, referring to time
To advance towards someone to be with them, to listen to them or to see them
Figuratively: to become accessible, within reach
To come near to God, to establish a relationship with Him
G1448.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial: to physically draw closer to a place or a person (Luke 19:41: Jesus approaches the city of Jerusalem; Acts 22:6: Paul draws near to Damascus on the road). It is the movement of the body that decreases the distance.

2. The word also describes the imminent arrival of an event: time moving towards a decisive moment, as in "the day is approaching" (Romans 13:12) or "the hour is approaching" (Matthew 26:45). It is time drawing closer to us.

3. For the Christian faith, the word becomes richer: when it is said that "the kingdom of heaven is near" (Matthew 3:2, Mark 1:15), it announces not only a future event but a reality that is drawing near and becoming accessible. God's salvation is no longer distant; it comes to meet man.

4. The word also describes the action of personally advancing towards someone: tax collectors draw near to Jesus to hear him (Luke 15:1), seeking his company and teaching.

5. In spiritual language, drawing near to God (Hebrews 7:19, James 4:8) means establishing a personal relationship with Him, becoming close to Him through prayer and faith. It is to break down the barrier that separates us from Him.
G1448.origine: The word comes from the root ἐγγύς (engús: near, close) and literally means "to make near" or "to come close." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates נגשׁ (nagash) or קרב (qarav), which carry the same sense of drawing near. The word family also includes the noun ἐγγύτης (proximity) and the adjective ἐγγύς (near). It is a simple and ancient word, fundamental for expressing movement and relationship.
G1448.emploi: The word ἐγγίζω appears 42 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke who favors it. It is divided into two main uses: spatial first (to approach a city, a person in the narrative: Luke 19:41, 24:15, Acts 22:6), and temporal second (the arrival of a moment: day, hour, end of times). This second use is crucial in the announcement of the kingdom: Jesus and the apostles proclaim that the kingdom of God "is near" (Matthew 3:2, 4:17, Mark 1:15), which means it is visibly manifesting, that the messianic times are beginning. Finally, in the spiritual sense, drawing near to God (Hebrews 7:19, James 4:8) becomes the condition for an intimate relationship with the Lord. The word thus evolves from the concrete (space) to the abstract (time, the kingdom, the relationship with God), but always on the model of drawing near.
G1448.portee: For the Christian, this word carries a fundamental hope: the kingdom of God is not a distant or theoretical reality; it comes to meet men and becomes accessible. Moreover, the verb to draw near invites everyone to voluntarily approach God in prayer and obedience, through the mediation of Jesus who has abolished the distance. It is a call to urgency: if the Lord is drawing near, if the end of times is approaching (1 Peter 4:7), then the Christian life must be lived with vigilance and faithfulness. The word reminds us that God is never far from those who sincerely seek Him.

sens: To mark letters or words on a surface
To inscribe in an official register
To be engraved in someone's consciousness or memory
G1449.detail:
1. The verb primarily denotes the material action of writing: tracing characters on a surface to leave a lasting mark. It is to paint or engrave letters, as one would do on papyrus or parchment. The idea is that of something that is imprinted and remains visible.
2. In an administrative sense, "to write" means to record, to inscribe someone or something in an official public register, as one would do to list citizens or candidates. It is to give a status, a recognized place.
3. Spiritually, the word takes on a transferred meaning: our names are "written in heaven" (Luke 10:20), not with ink, but permanently engraved in divine memory and in the hearts of believers (2 Corinthians 3:2). It is the image of an indelible mark, not only visible but deeply imprinted.
G1449.origine: The Greek verb "to write" (engraphō) is composed of the prefix "en-" (in, on) and the root "graphō" (to trace, to paint, to write). It literally evokes the action of tracing something "in" or "on" a surface. The root "graphō" is the same that gives in French the words "graphic," "writing," and "graffiti." The basic meaning is always concrete: to leave a visible and lasting trace.
G1449.emploi: The verb "to write" appears three times in the New Testament, always in the passive voice ("to be written"), which emphasizes the idea of something being engraved, imposed from the outside. In Luke 10:20, Jesus speaks of the names of the disciples "written in heaven": it is a promise of salvation and belonging to the kingdom of God, a definitive and heavenly inscription. In 2 Corinthians 3:2-3, Paul uses the image to describe the Corinthians themselves as a letter "written" in hearts, and especially as a letter of Christ not written with ink but by the Spirit of the living God. The contrast between "ink" and "the Spirit," between the "table of stone" and the "table of flesh" shows that biblical writing evokes the transition from the old regime (the Law engraved in stone) to the new regime (grace written in hearts).
G1449.portee: This word reminds the Christian that their belonging to God is not temporary or forgettable: it is inscribed, engraved in an indelible manner. The believer is not an anonymous person, but someone whose name is "written in heaven." Moreover, the image of the letter "written" by the Spirit in hearts invites the reader to see their own life as a message from God to the world: not a document engraved on dead stone, but a living reality, transformed by the action of the Holy Spirit.

sens: One who takes responsibility for an obligation on behalf of another person
One who guarantees the solidity or validity of a covenant or commitment
G1450.detail:
1. A guarantor is someone who answers for another person in case of failure: they personally take on the responsibility of a debt or a promise. It is like an intermediary who commits their honor and goods to ensure that a commitment will be fulfilled (Hebrews 7:22).
2. In a spiritual and theological sense, a guarantor is one who makes a covenant credible and solid by guaranteeing its fulfillment. Jesus is called the guarantor of a better covenant: he commits his person, his sacrifice, his faithfulness so that everyone can be assured that God will keep His word towards us.
G1450.origine: The Greek word ἔγγυος comes from a root that means "pledge" or "surety." It originally designates one who deposits a valuable object to ensure the execution of a contract. The word belongs to the legal and commercial vocabulary of antiquity: it is a legal term that later passes into the theological domain to describe the certainty brought by Jesus Christ to the new covenant.
G1450.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 7:22. This letter, written to show the superiority of Christ over the Old Testament, uses it to affirm that Jesus guarantees a better covenant than the old one. The context is that of Christ's eternal priesthood and his unique sacrifice: his permanent presence with God is the greatest guarantee that a covenant can have. The word suggests here that Jesus personally takes on the responsibility for the perfect execution of the new covenant.
G1450.portee: For the Christian reader, this word conveys something deeply comforting: it is not our efforts or our faithfulness that uphold the covenant with God; it is Jesus Christ himself. He personally answers for it. We can rest on this absolute, unshakeable guarantee offered by the one who is forever interceding for us before the Father.

sens: at a short distance in space
in a short time interval, imminent
spiritually or relationally close to someone
G1451.detail:
1. Near describes what is at a short distance: summer is near when the fig tree's leaves begin to grow (Matthew 24:32), or Lydda is near Joppa (Acts 9:38). It is a matter of measurable geographical proximity.
2. The word also applies to time: a feast that is about to arrive, like the Passover which was near (John 6:4), or the kingdom of God which was believed to be about to appear at any moment (Luke 19:11). The event is approaching, it is about to happen.
3. Finally, near can express a personal or spiritual relationship: the believers from the Gentiles have become near to God through Christ, while others were far away (Ephesians 2:13 and 2:17). Here, it is not a physical distance, but access to the Lord, intimacy with Him.
G1451.origine: The Greek word engus comes from a root that evokes the idea of closeness, proximity. The Hebrew קָרוֹב (qarov), which this Greek word often translates in the Greek Old Testament, carries the same meaning: what is near, what approaches. The family of this word also includes the comparative "nearer" and the superlative "nearest."
G1451.emploi: Engus appears about thirty times in the New Testament, especially in John, Matthew, and Luke. It is first used for concrete distances: places that are near each other (John 3:23, John 11:18, Acts 1:12, Acts 9:38). Then, it designates approaching moments: Jewish feasts (John 2:13, John 6:4, John 7:2), the coming of the kingdom (Matthew 24:32-33, Luke 21:30-31), or the day of the Lord (Revelation 1:3, Philippians 4:5). Finally, it takes on a spiritual meaning: through Christ, the formerly distant Gentiles have become near to God (Ephesians 2:13, Ephesians 2:17), and the Word of God is near to us (Romans 10:8).
G1451.portee: This word speaks to us of presence and accessibility: first, it reminds us that the return of Christ and the fulfillment of His reign are real and coming, not indefinitely distant. Next, it reveals that the relationship with God is not inaccessible: through Christ, the barriers have fallen, and God is near to us, not far away.

sens: At a shorter distance in space
At a shorter time interval
Approaching more towards its fulfillment
G1452.detail:
1. The word designates what is located at a reduced distance: Paul says that salvation is "closer" to us, meaning it is drawing near (Romans 13:11). It is the comparison between two distances: salvation was far, it is now closer to its final realization.
2. In terms of time, it expresses that something is approaching: an expected event is drawing closer to the present moment, like a deadline that is decreasing.
3. Figuratively, the word describes a spiritual reality that is progressing towards us: the day of the Lord, the end times, judgment — all eschatological realities that are getting closer day by day.
G1452.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἐγγύς (engús, "near"), and ἐγγύτερος is its comparative form ("closer"). This root commonly translates the Hebrew קָרוֹב (qaróv) in the Greek Old Testament. The suffix -τερος marks the comparison: it compares two distances or two states of proximity.
G1452.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 13:11. Paul uses it to exhort the Roman Christians to awaken spiritually, for the return of the Lord and the fulfillment of salvation are becoming more imminent with the passage of time. It is a word of eschatological vigilance: the more days pass, the closer the decisive moment approaches, and we must take this into account to adjust our conduct.
G1452.portee: This word invites the Christian to live in conscious expectation of the return of Christ. The closer the end approaches, the more the urgency becomes real: it is not a distant abstraction, but a reality that is drawing near. This should change our way of living daily, awaken us from spiritual lethargy, and push us towards obedience and holiness.

sens: To awaken someone who is sleeping or resting
To raise someone who is lying down, who is sick
To bring forth, to evoke, to manifest
To raise an opposition, hostility
To build, to erect a building
G1453.detail:
1. To awaken from sleep or rest: the word describes the physical action of pulling someone from sleep. Joseph awoke (Matthew 1:24) receives in a dream the command of an angel and wakes up to act; likewise, the virgins rise from their sleep (Matthew 25:7).
2. To raise someone who is lying down, sick, or weak: Jesus raises Peter's mother-in-law who had a fever (Mark 1:31), or He commands the paralyzed man to get up (Mark 2:11) — the body stands up, the person resumes activity.
3. To bring back to life, to resurrect the dead: this is the most frequent meaning in the New Testament. Jesus raises the dead (John 5:21), notably He Himself is raised from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:12), an image of the passage from death to eternal life.
4. To bring forth, to evoke, to manifest: God raised King David (Acts 13:22) or brings forth children to Abraham (Matthew 3:9), giving form and existence to what was not yet.
5. To oppose, to raise against: nations will rise against each other (Matthew 24:7), expressing a rising, a hostility.
6. To build, to erect a building: Jesus speaks of His body as a temple to be raised (John 2:19-20), in a sense of reconstruction or restoration.
G1453.origine: The verb comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of lifting, straightening, standing up. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb קוּם (koum), which means to rise, to stand, to surge — a very concrete image of the body moving from horizontal (lying down, dead, asleep) to vertical (standing, alive, awake). This image of rising accompanies the word in all its uses, whether it concerns sleep, illness, death, or an action that rises.
G1453.emploi: The word appears 137 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its meaning varies according to the context: it first designates the awakening from sleep or the raising of a sickbed (Mark 4:38, John 5:8), then the raising of the dead — the resurrection of Jesus in particular, the key to the Christian faith (Matthew 17:9, 1 Corinthians 15:12). The word also takes on the meaning of to evoke, to bring forth (Acts 13:22: God raised David), to oppose or to raise (Matthew 24:7: nations will rise), and even to build a structure (John 2:19: to raise the temple). This versatility reflects the underlying image: moving from a low position to a high position, from inactivity to action.
G1453.portee: For the Christian, this word is at the heart of hope: the resurrection of Jesus, signified by ἐγείρω, is the foundation of his own hope of resurrection. It is not a dream or mythology, but a concrete reality — the body that had lain in death stands again in eternal life. It is also a word of power: God who awakens the dead also awakens the sleeping heart, raises it from its degradation, and brings forth in it a new life. The image of rising speaks to every Christian: rising from indifference, from falling, to stand firm in faith.

sens: Action de se relever, de se réveiller
Retour à la vie après la mort
G1454.detail: 1. The word primarily describes the physical action of rising up or waking up: someone who stands up after having been lying down. This is the primary image of the Greek word « egersis », which comes from the verb « egeirô » meaning « to wake up » or « to raise ». 2. In the Bible, this word specifically refers to the return to life after death. In Matthew 27:53, after the resurrection of Jesus, the tombs are opened and the dead come out of their graves to enter the holy city: it is the power of Jesus' resurrection that brings them back to life.
G1454.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « egeirô » (to wake up, to lift, to raise) and carries the image of a person being awakened from sleep or being raised up. This root expresses the action of moving from inactivity to activity, from rest to movement. In Hebrew, this notion often corresponds to the verb « qûm » (to rise, to stand up), which the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses in parallel contexts.
G1454.emploi: This word appears only once in the French New Testament: in Matthew 27:53. At this key moment in the Passion narrative, Matthew reports that after Jesus' death on the cross and his resurrection, the tombs of the saints who had died are opened and these dead come out of their graves to enter the holy city and appear to many. The word « egersis » (resurrection) here designates the miraculous event by which God brings the dead back to life. It is a divine act that testifies to Jesus' victory over death and anticipates the final resurrection of all believers.
G1454.portee: For the Christian, this word carries the hope of eternal life: resurrection is not a theological abstraction, but the concrete power of God that conquers death. Matthew's account shows that Jesus' resurrection is not isolated: it frees the dead and transforms reality. This promise assures the believer that, just as Jesus was raised from the dead, those who belong to him will experience the same resurrection and the same new life.

sens: personne envoyée en secret pour observer et rapporter
personne qui se cache ou qui guette dans l'intention de nuire
agent provocateur qui feint une apparence trompeuse
G1455.detail: 1. The word designates someone who has secretly slipped somewhere to observe: in Luke 20:20, Jesus' adversaries send « people » who pretend to be righteous but who are actually watching him secretly to catch his words. 2. It also refers to someone who is lurking, hidden or still, waiting for the right moment to strike: the image evokes someone who is ambushed. 3. The meaning extends to one who uses cunning and falsehood: they present themselves in a false light (here, « righteous ») to carry out a malicious mission (to set a trap).
G1455.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἐγκαθίημι (« to place inside, to ambush »), composed of ἐν (« in ») and κάθημαι (« to sit »). The basic image is that of someone sitting or placing themselves inside to watch. The root evokes hidden waiting, an ambush. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, words like אָרַב (« ambush ») express a comparable idea.
G1455.emploi: The word appears only once in Luke 20:20. The Jewish religious leaders send these « people » spies to secretly watch Jesus, hoping to catch him in a fault. They disguise themselves under the appearance of piety (« pretended to be righteous ») so that Jesus would not suspect them, then they would aim to extract from his words an accusation to bring before the civil authorities.
G1455.portee: This passage shows how hostility towards Jesus was organized into a strategy of deception and surveillance. The believer sees here a biblical warning about the danger of deceptive appearances and the cunning of evil: true discernment is not superficial. It is also a reminder that Jesus, aware of these traps, continued his ministry without fear, offering a model of trust in God in the face of hostility.

sens: Fête commémorant la consécration ou la purification d'un lieu sacré
Chez les Juifs, fête annuelle célébrant la purification du Temple après sa profanation par Antiochus Épiphane
G1456.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the action of dedicating a building, solemnly consecrating it to God — and it is this moment of purification that is then celebrated each year. In the Old Testament, the dedication of the Tabernacle and the Temple was marked by special sacrifices (see Numbers 7). 2. Among the Jews of the New Testament period, the Dedication (Hanukkah) was the anniversary celebration of the rededication and purification of the Temple, desecrated centuries earlier by the Syrian king Antiochus Epiphanes. It is during this winter festival that Jesus walks in the Temple in Jerusalem (John 10:22).
G1456.origine: The Greek word comes from « en » (ἐν) and « new » (καινός), with the suffix -ία: literally « renewal ». It is a term very close to the ancient Jewish practice: in Hebrew, it was called hanoukkah, which also means « inauguration » or « consecration ». The Greek translators of the Old Testament used this word to render the festivals of consecration of the Temple and the Tabernacle.
G1456.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in John 10:22. Jesus is in Jerusalem during the winter, at the festival of Dedication. This detail suggests that Jesus participated in this Jewish festival while remaining critical of the religious authorities of the Temple. This mention situates the text in the precise context of Jewish religious practices in the first century.
G1456.portee: The mention of the Dedication reminds the reader that Jesus did not reject legitimate Jewish practices, but that he was part of the continuity of Israel's faith. It is also in this place that he affirms his identity as Messiah (John 10:24-25). For the believer, this shows the importance of celebrating, in their own practices, what dedicates life to God — not out of conformity, but through a renewed acknowledgment of his presence.

sens: Mettre en route, commencer quelque chose de nouveau
Renouveler, donner une vie nouvelle
Consacrer solennellement par une cérémonie
G1457.detail: 1. The verb primarily means « to set in motion » or « to begin »: it conveys the idea of launching something new. This is why it can mean « to innovate » — bringing something new into the world. 2. It can also mean « to renew » or « to make new »: to restore something that is old or deteriorated. For example, one can renew the heart by purifying it (as in the psalms). 3. The most frequently encountered meaning in biblical Greek, especially in connection with the Old Testament, is « to inaugurate » or « to consecrate »: that is, to solemnly put something into service, usually through a religious ceremony. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, Paul states that the old covenant was « inaugurated » with blood (Hebrews 9:18), and that Jesus has « inaugurated » a new and living way (Hebrews 10:20) — a completely new access to God.
G1457.origine: The word is formed from the preposition « en » (ἐν) and the verb « to make new » (καινίζω), which itself comes from the adjective « new » (καινός). The image is that of renewal or beginning. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb generally renders the Hebrew « to consecrate » (חנך, hanak in Hebrew, from which the English Hanukkah, the festival of Dedication, also derives), which evokes the inauguration of the Temple or an altar.
G1457.emploi: This verb appears very rarely in the New Testament (only twice in the Epistle to the Hebrews). It is used to describe the solemn inauguration of the new covenant in Jesus Christ. In Hebrews 9:18, Paul explains that the old covenant had to be inaugurated with blood, according to the Law; in Hebrews 10:20, he asserts that Jesus has opened and inaugurated a new and living way to God. The word emphasizes the official and liturgical nature of these two covenants.
G1457.portee: This verb reminds the believer that Jesus did not merely abolish the old covenant: he inaugurated something radically new. This « new and living way » (Hebrews 10:20) is not a simple reform, but a completely new opening of access to God, through his death and resurrection. It is an invitation to enter into what God inaugurates, rather than remaining attached to the old religious system.

sens: To call someone to justice, to bring them before a court
To bring an accusation against someone, to charge them with a fault or a crime
To be the object of an accusation, of a complaint
G1458.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to call someone to appear in court, to summon them before a tribunal. In Acts 19:38, it refers to officially "complaining about someone" — the workers of Demetrius could "appeal to justice" against one another if they had a dispute.

2. More broadly, it means to bring a formal accusation against someone, to charge them with a fault, an offense, or a crime. Paul fears in Acts 19:40 of being "accused of sedition" for the gathering; in Acts 23:28, the commander wants to know the reason for which the Jews "accuse" him; in Acts 23:29, Paul is "accused regarding matters related to their law".

3. It also refers to the state of one who is under accusation. Paul says in Acts 26:2: "I stand here to make my defense against all the things of which I am accused by the Jews" — he bears the accusation upon himself and must defend himself.
G1458.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix "ἐν" (in, within) and the verb "καλέω" (to call). It literally means "to call in" — that is, to call someone before justice, into the tribunal. In Romans 8:33, we also find "κατηγορέω" (to accuse before) and "αἰτίαομαι" (to declare guilty), synonyms that are more or less close depending on the context.
G1458.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the Greek New Testament, almost always in Acts (6 times) and once in Romans. It almost exclusively describes judicial or legal accusations. In Acts 19:38, it concerns a civil recourse before the court; in Acts 23:28-29, it refers to Paul's accusation by the Jews before Roman justice; in Acts 26:2, Paul defends himself against the accusations made against him. The construction varies: with the dative of the accused person (Acts 19:38), or in the passive "to be accused of" with a genitive of the thing reproached (Acts 19:40: accused of sedition; Acts 23:29: accused regarding their law). It is always a serious, judicial, or official context.
G1458.portee: This verb reminds us that an accusation is never trivial: it engages a procedure, it requires a defense. For the reader, it is an invitation not to accuse lightly, and to submit to the true justice of God rather than to the accusations of men. In Romans 8:33, God Himself is the one who justifies and who alone can truly "accuse" — which gives the Christian liberation in the face of human accusations.

sens: To leave behind, to cease holding or keeping something
To leave someone alone, without support, without defense
To break a promise of support to someone
To cease attending a place or gathering
G1459.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to leave behind: in Romans 9:29, God leaves a remnant to Israel, a "posterity" that survives despite judgment.

2. But the word takes on its full force when it describes the abandonment of a person. It is when someone else abandons you that you are left to yourself, without help. Jesus cries these words on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34). The word evokes the terrible experience of feeling alone, without the support of the one you relied on.

3. It can also mean to cease a promise or commitment to someone. In Hebrews 13:5, God assures: "I will never forsake you," meaning: I will not break my covenant or my support. It is a solemn promise.

4. The word also applies to forsaking a place, a gathering. In Hebrews 10:25, the author reproaches some Christians for "forsaking" their common meeting, that is, ceasing to gather with others.
G1459.origine: The Greek word combines a particle (ἐν-, "in") and a root that fundamentally means "to leave, to abandon." The underlying root evokes the action of turning away or distancing oneself. This verb often translates the Hebrew עזב (hazab), "to leave, to abandon," which appears as early as the Old Testament to describe rejection or forgetfulness. The intensive prefix reinforces the idea: this is not a simple departure, but a complete abandonment, a rupture.
G1459.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the New Testament, primarily in a context of abandonment or desertion. Its most poignant use is in the mouth of Jesus at Gethsemane and on the cross (Matthew, Mark), where it evokes the feeling of being delivered to suffering without recourse. In Acts and the epistles, it describes either the rejection of God's promise towards the faithful (Acts 2:27, quoted from the Psalms), or the persecutions that Christians endure without being "forsaken" by God (2 Corinthians 4:9), or the failure of men to fulfill their duties (2 Timothy 4:10, 4:16) and the absence of the faithful from the assembly (Hebrews 10:25). In Romans 9:29, it carries a more positive sense: God does not allow all of Israel to perish, He preserves a remnant.
G1459.portee: This word reminds the believer of a fundamental truth: God, unlike men, never abandons us (Hebrews 13:5). Even when we go through suffering and feel the apparent absence of God (like Jesus on the cross), we are not truly left to ourselves. It is a word that comforts and roots faith, not by negating suffering, but by assuring a faithful presence. It also engages the believer: not to forsake the assembly of the saints is to recognize that the Christian community is a precious good and a necessary mutual support.

sens: To dwell, to live among a people, a community
To be established in a place, at the heart of a population
(figuratively) To be confronted with, to experience the reality of what surrounds
G1460.detail:
1. The word denotes the act of physically dwelling in the midst of a group of people, having one's habitat there. In 2 Peter 2:8, Lot "dwelt among" the Sodomites: he lived among them, sharing their daily environment, even if he did not share their sins.
2. It means to be established in a specific place, rooted in a community. The image is of someone who is not just passing through, but who settles down and lives there.
3. By extension, it means to be involved in, to be exposed to the concrete reality of what is happening around oneself. Lot dwelling among the Sodomites was confronted day after day with the criminal acts he saw and heard.
G1460.origine: The word combines two elements: ἐν (in, within) and κατοικέω (to dwell, to reside). It comes from κάτα (down, according to) and οἶκος (the house). The basic image is that of settling in a house, in a place, fixing one's stay there. The prefix ἐν reinforces the idea: not only to dwell, but to dwell among, at the heart of.
G1460.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:8. The apostle Peter uses it to describe Lot's situation in Sodom: living among the inhabitants of the city, Lot was daily tormented by the sight of their sins. This context shows that "to dwell among" does not mean to approve of the behavior of others, but to be involved in their reality, to be exposed to and affected by it. It is a word that emphasizes the isolation of the righteous within an ungodly society.
G1460.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian often lives in a hostile or unbelieving environment, caught between their faith and the reality of the world around them. Like Lot, they may be "tormented" by what they see and hear, without being able to escape completely. It is an image of empathy towards those who seek to remain faithful amid a context of sin and corruption.

sens: To graft a branch onto a tree by joining living wood
To incorporate someone into a group to which they did not naturally belong
G1461.detail:
1. In the concrete sense of gardening, "graft" means to take a branch and join it to the living wood of another tree so that it grows with it and bears fruit. It is a manual operation that unites two distinct elements. In Romans 11:17, Paul speaks of a wild olive tree that has been "grafted" in place of the natural branches that were cut off: the image comes from the agricultural world and remains very vivid.
2. In a figurative sense, the word refers to the incorporation of a person or group into a whole to which they did not originally belong. Paul uses it to describe how the Gentiles, strangers to the Israel of the living God, have been "grafted" in place of Israelites who rejected Christ, and how Israel itself can be "grafted in again" despite its unbelief (Romans 11:19, 23, 24). The underlying idea is that of an established connection, of new participation and communion.
G1461.origine: The word comes from the root "kentrizō" (to graft), preceded by the preposition "en" (in). The image is horticultural: it refers to the common practice in the Mediterranean of grafting branches of fresh shoots onto old trunks to improve the harvest or renew an aging tree. Paul borrows this metaphor to explain how God integrates the Gentiles into the people of the covenant and how He can restore Israel.
G1461.emploi: The word appears only in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11, in the great allegory of the olive tree where Paul explains the relationship between Israel and the nations. It appears four times in Romans 11:17, 19, 23, and 24, always in the passive voice or in a context of divine action: the Gentiles "have been grafted in," Israel "will be grafted in again." The meaning remains constant: it is always about the insertion of a branch (literally or figuratively of a people) into a living organism from which it receives nourishment and life. The repetition emphasizes the theological importance of the message.
G1461.portee: This word reminds us that our belonging to the family of God is not due to a natural superiority, but to a grafting, that is, to the free act of God. Like the wild olive grafted onto the cultivated olive, we are incorporated into a story that surpasses us. This image also invites the Gentile to humility: the cultivated tree could remove us as it has cut off certain branches. And it assures Israel that God has not definitively rejected it: He can "graft it in again" if it believes.

sens: Reproach, grievance made against someone
Charge brought before the justice system
Guilt or fault attested
G1462.detail:
1. The word refers to a reproach directed at someone, a word that incriminates them. In Acts 23:29, Paul is presented as "accused concerning questions related to their law": it is the very act of accusing that is described.
2. It is also a formal charge, a legal accusation brought before the courts. Acts 25:16 speaks of it as serious matters: "the accused" must "have the ability to defend themselves against the things they are accused of." The accusation here is a legal grievance, examined by the judge.
3. By extension, it also refers to the guilt itself, that for which someone can be legally condemned. In Acts 23:29, Paul "had committed no crime deserving death"—it is the absence of serious guilt that is emphasized.
G1462.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ἐγκαλέω (to call against oneself, to accuse), formed from ἐν (in, against) and καλέω (to call). It literally means "a call against someone." The Greek word often translates the Hebrew notion of legal accusation in the Old Testament. The root evokes the idea of "bringing a charge against," of "summoning someone to court."
G1462.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both passages taken from the Acts of the Apostles, in the account of Paul's trial in Caesarea. In Acts 23:29, the Roman tribune notes that Paul is accused, but that his accusers have no serious crime to prove against him. In Acts 25:16, Governor Festus states the principle of Roman justice: before condemning, the accused must be able to confront their accusers and defend themselves. Both uses are strictly judicial: the accusation is a legal formality, not mere gossip.
G1462.portee: For the Christian, these verses remind us that even in the face of persecution, God protects the right to defend oneself. Paul, falsely accused, can seek justice according to Roman law itself. It is an encouragement: the truth can be established, and false accusations can be refuted by testimony and word. No accusation without evidence carries the weight of real guilt.

sens: To put on a garment, to cover oneself
To wear as armor or service equipment
To adopt an inner quality as one puts on a garment
G1463.detail:
1. The word describes the physical action of putting a garment on oneself, of covering oneself. The image comes from a knot (the root word κόμβος means "knot"): one ties a garment around oneself, generally an apron or a work tunic worn by servants. It is a concrete and daily gesture.

2. Specifically, it evokes the garment tied on for service — that of the servant who prepares to serve, who equips themselves for the task. The apron or the garment one puts on changes your status: you now present yourself as someone in service to another.

3. Figuratively, the word applies to attitude and inner qualities: one can "clothe" oneself with humility, that is, adopt it not as a mere passing feeling, but as a garment that one consciously puts on, that one visibly wears. This is what 1 Peter 5:5 asks: clothe yourselves with humility in your mutual relationships.
G1463.origine: The verb comes from κόμβος (kompos, "knot"), from which ἐγκόμβωμα (the garment tied with a knot, particularly the servant's apron) derives. The preposition ἐν (in) intensifies the action: "to tie oneself in," to equip oneself. The word emphasizes less the garment itself than the voluntary act of tying it on oneself, of making it one's equipment.
G1463.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:5, in the imperative: Peter exhorts young Christians and all believers to "clothe" themselves with humility toward one another. The context shows that humility is not a superficial posture, but an active reality that must be embraced, like the servant putting on their apron before working. It is a deliberate choice, a concrete practice to be implemented in the Christian community.
G1463.portee: This word invites the Christian to see humility not as a vague feeling or an abstract virtue, but as something to be put on, to be worn like a service armor. Just as the servant concretely equips themselves for their task, the believer must equip themselves with humility before entering into relationships with others. It is a call to move from words to action, to a visible and practical humility.

sens: Obstacle, hindrance, that which blocks passage or progress
That which interrupts or stops a process
That which prevents or slows down something from being accomplished
G1464.detail:
1. The word "obstacle" literally refers to something that cuts, slices, or creates an interruption. It is a hindrance, a blockage that stops or slows down progress: in 1 Corinthians 9:12, Paul states that he renounces his right to be supported by the Church "so as not to create an obstacle to the Gospel."

2. Metaphorically, it refers to anything that can hinder, obstruct, or slow down: Paul refuses to allow anything to obstruct the spread of the Good News. The obstacle can be material, social, or moral — anything that could divert people from the Christian message.
G1464.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means a "cut" or an "incision" — the image of a blade that cuts, that interrupts. The verb from the same family, "ἐγκόπτω" (enkoptô), means "to obstruct," "to hinder," "to interrupt." This notion of interruption, of breaking the normal flow, is at the heart of the word: an obstacle cuts the road, breaks the momentum.
G1464.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Corinthians 9:12. Paul uses it to explain his choice not to live at the expense of the Church, despite his right as an apostle. He refuses to let his livelihood be an "obstacle" that could disturb or scandalize some, thereby weakening the impact of the message of the Gospel. It is a term that signals a pastoral concern: how to do nothing that could hinder the faith or conversion of others.
G1464.portee: This word reminds the believer that personal freedom is not an end in itself. Like Paul, we are called to ask ourselves: is there in my conduct, in my choices, something that could hinder the Gospel or disturb the faith of another? It is a call to responsibility, gentleness, and wisdom: to accept renouncing a legitimate right so that nothing blocks the progress of the Good News.

sens: To interrupt or slow down someone's physical progress
To create an obstacle to an action or movement
To obstruct the realization of a plan or obligation
To disturb, hinder, or delay someone in an endeavor
G1465.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to cut or interrupt the way: it is like placing an obstacle on the road to stop someone who is advancing. In Galatians 5:7, Paul asks: "Who hindered you from obeying the truth?" — the image is that of a runner being blocked mid-race.

2. The word then extends to anything that hinders, disturbs, or delays an action. In Acts 24:4, Tertullus tells Governor Felix: "Not to detain you any longer," meaning not to prolong his hearing unnecessarily.

3. The idea deepens further: to prevent becomes to obstruct a project, a desire, or a duty. Paul writes in Romans 15:22: "This is what has often hindered me from coming to you" — not by brute force, but by circumstances that constrained his plan.

4. The word can also mean to cause harm or inconvenience. In 1 Peter 3:7, "let nothing hinder your prayers" suggests that the mistreatment of women by their husbands hinders even the couple's prayer life.
G1465.origine: The Greek word is composed of "en" (in, inside) and "koptô" (to cut, to strike). The starting image is therefore literal: to cut or strike from within, that is, to interrupt a progression. This root "koptô" evokes the act of splitting, breaking an object or a continuous path. The prefix "en" reinforces the idea of an action that blocks from the inside or along the way.
G1465.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul's epistles. In Acts 24:4, Tertullus seeks not to detain the governor too long. In Romans 15:22 and 1 Thessalonians 2:18, Paul uses the word to describe the obstacles that prevented him from visiting the churches: these are not deliberate refusals, but contrary circumstances. In Galatians 5:7, the apostle uses a sports image: the church in Galatia "was running well," but something "hindered" or "prevented" it from obeying the truth. In 1 Peter 3:7, the word takes on a broader meaning: unjust conduct in marriage can "hinder" the couple's prayer life. The usage therefore varies from temporal slowing to blocking a spiritual endeavor.
G1465.portee: This word reminds the believer that obstacles can arise on the path of the Christian life — some come from outside, others from within ourselves, and still others from spiritual hostility. It invites us to examine what hinders our spiritual progress and our obedience to the truth, and to seek to overcome them. For couples, 1 Peter 3:7 warns that injustice deprives even prayer of its effectiveness: it is a call to live in harmony so that nothing blocks communion with God.

sens: Self-control, mastery over one's appetites and desires
Virtue that restrains from excess in eating, drinking, and pleasures
Moderation and wisdom in all behaviors
Fruit of the Holy Spirit in the believer
G1466.detail:
1. The word first denotes the self-mastery one exercises over oneself, the ability to dominate oneself: it is to keep control over one's instincts and passions rather than surrendering to them (Galatians 5:23).
2. It specifically concerns moderation in eating and drinking: temperance is the art of not exceeding the measure, of remaining wise in the face of bodily pleasures and the temptations they present.
3. More broadly, it is the wisdom that permeates all choices and actions: it restrains the tongue, gestures, thoughts, it masters anger and pride.
4. In apostolic teaching, temperance is a virtue that the Holy Spirit develops in the believer (Galatians 5:23), and it is progressively acquired in a chain: after knowledge comes temperance, and after temperance comes patience (2 Peter 1:6).
G1466.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "strong, powerful" (the same as the word for "mastery"). It is formed from the prefix "en" (inside) and the word for "strength" or "power": thus, temperance is the power one exercises over oneself, from within. It is a well-known virtue in ancient Greece, but it takes on a new meaning in the Gospel when it becomes a gift of the Holy Spirit rather than a mere human discipline.
G1466.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the epistles and Acts. In Acts 24:25, Paul preaches it to Felix: it accompanies justice and the coming judgment, and it seems terrifying to the governor. In Galatians 5:23, Paul lists it among the fruits of the Spirit — the virtues that the Holy Spirit produces in the believer — alongside love, peace, and gentleness. In 2 Peter 1:6, it is part of a chain of spiritual growth: it is a virtue that one arrives at after knowledge and cultivates to achieve patience. It is never presented as an isolated human effort, but always as a divine work within us.
G1466.portee: Temperance reminds the Christian that he is not a slave to his desires and that God gives him the power to master his body and instincts. It is a virtue of freedom: it liberates us from the grip of the flesh. It also reminds us that a Christian life is not primarily about austere sacrifice, but about a growing participation in the life of the Spirit, which restores to us the mastery of ourselves — that which sin had taken away.

sens: To exercise mastery over one's desires and passions
To practice abstinence, to refrain from what is permitted but dangerous
To demonstrate discipline and self-control
G1467.detail:
1. The word describes the action of mastering and controlling one's carnal passions. It is an inner strength that restrains one who might be carried away by desire. In 1 Corinthians 7:9, Paul says that if someone lacks self-control (that is, if he cannot master himself), it is better for him to marry than to remain consumed by desire.
2. The word also means to voluntarily practice abstinence — to deprive oneself of what is allowed to achieve a nobler goal. In 1 Corinthians 9:25, Paul compares the one who runs for a perishable crown to the Christian who imposes all sorts of abstinences upon himself to obtain an eternal crown. It is a chosen discipline, a voluntary effort.
G1467.origine: The word comes from a Greek term meaning "powerful" or "master." The compound form evokes the idea of being master of oneself, possessing control over one's own strengths. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew meaning "to restrain" or "to master" (as in Genesis 43:31 where Joseph controls himself so as not to weep).
G1467.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letters. In 1 Corinthians 7:9, it describes the inability of some to master their sexual desire. In 1 Corinthians 9:25, Paul uses the same verb to speak of the self-discipline of the committed Christian. In both cases, Paul addresses the domination of bodily passions, either through marriage or through ascetic discipline in view of an eternal reward. The context shows that this self-control is a central virtue for the Christian.
G1467.portee: This word reminds the Christian that spiritual life requires real self-control, not mere passive abstention. It is not a denial of the body, but rather its governance in service to God. For Paul, this discipline is motivated by an eternal prize: incontinence distances us from our goal, while mastery brings us closer. It is not an end in itself, but a means to serve the Lord with all our being.

sens: Who masters his appetites and passions
Who exercises restraint and moderation in his desires
Who shows personal discipline in the face of temptations
G1468.detail:
1. The word speaks of someone who keeps his appetites in check — who is not dominated by hunger, thirst, carnal desire, or any other bodily craving. It is an inward-directed strength of will.

2. More broadly, temperance extends to all areas of life: one can be temperate in speech (not speaking without thinking), in spending (not wasting), in anger (not losing one's temper). It is a wise restraint in the face of the constant solicitations that surround us.

3. In Titus 1:8, Paul describes the qualities of a church leader: he must be temperate. This means he cannot be a slave to alcohol, lust, or money — in short, to ordinary passions that would tear at his testimony and moral authority. It is a condition for leading God's people.
G1468.origine: The word comes from "κράτος" (kratos), which means "strength" or "power" — the idea of mastering or dominating. Here, the prefix "ἐν" (en) reinforces this notion: it is a strength directed towards oneself, an authority exercised over one's own desires. The word implies that appetites are a real power that must be governed with courage, like a warrior mastering his adversaries.
G1468.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:8, where Paul establishes the criteria for an elder to be recognized as such. It is placed between "just" and "holy," forming a triad of essential moral virtues. The Bible emphasizes that temperance is not a passive virtue (abstaining out of weakness), but active and vigorous: it is the strong man who governs himself. It is particularly important for one who teaches or leads, as it guarantees his integrity and credibility with the flock.
G1468.portee: Temperance speaks to the heart of the modern Christian by reminding him that true freedom is not doing what one wants, but mastering one's desires in service of a godly life. It shows that true power is not imposing one's desires on others, but governing one's own passions. It is an invitation to joyful self-discipline, not out of fear or guilt, but because the Christian belongs to God.

sens: To place on the same level as
To compare oneself to
To categorize in the same group as
G1469.detail:
1. The word literally means "to count among" or "to rank in the same class as." It is the idea of placing someone or something on the same level as another, equating them in value or importance. In 2 Corinthians 10:12, Paul says he "dares not equal himself" to certain preachers who boast of themselves: he refuses to place himself on the same level as them.
2. By extension, the word expresses the act of comparing oneself to others, evaluating oneself in relation to other people. It is an act of judgment where one decides that two things or two people are equivalent or worthy of being paralleled. Paul suggests that this comparison between himself and these "super-apostles" would be inappropriate.
G1469.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἐν- ("in") and the verb κρίνω ("to judge," "to discern," "to decide"). It thus means "to classify within" or "to count among." This root κρίνω is very common in biblical Greek to express any act of judgment or evaluation. The word evokes the image of a judge who categorizes someone or something into a given category.
G1469.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 10:12. Paul uses it to refuse any comparison with the false apostles who commend themselves. He explains that "we do not dare to equal ourselves... to some who commend themselves." This unique occurrence in this polemical context shows that Paul considers such a parallel to be unwise and inappropriate. The word thus carries a critical connotation: to equal oneself with these deceptive preachers would be a judgment error.
G1469.portee: This verse speaks to us about an important spiritual vigilance: that of not deceiving ourselves by comparing our worth or legitimacy to that of people who boast of themselves or falsely claim authority. Paul invites us to resist the temptation to "equal" ourselves with those who lack honesty or true piety. It is also a call to wisdom in our judgments: some comparisons can mislead us.

sens: Place something inside another thing in such a way that it is not visible.
Mix an ingredient into a mass so that it diffuses.
G1470.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of concealing or hiding something by burying it inside: it is the gesture of someone who slips an object into the heart of another thing so that it disappears from view. In the parables of the leaven (Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21), the woman "puts" the leaven into the flour — she buries it within, in a sense hiding it in the mass of flour, so that it completely incorporates itself.
2. By extension, it also means to mix, to incorporate: the leaven does not remain visible on the surface; it must be placed at the heart of the flour for the entire dough to rise. The image is one of a discreet yet powerful action that works from within. It is this same action, in the parable, that causes the whole dough to transform — the leaven, hidden in the flour, makes it rise.
G1470.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἐν (in) and κρύπτω (to hide, to conceal). It literally means "to hide inside" or "to enclose within." This composition reflects the biblical idea that the Kingdom of God acts from within, in an invisible yet irreversible manner, just as leaven secretly works through the dough. The verb recalls the Hebrew root טמן (taman), which also means to bury or to hide.
G1470.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in two versions of the same parable: Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21. In both cases, Jesus describes the Kingdom of Heaven by comparing its action to that of leaven hidden in flour. The context is didactic — Jesus teaches through parables how the Kingdom develops discreetly and irresistibly in the world. The word translates the precise gesture of "putting" or "placing" the leaven into the flour, and the prefix ἐν- emphasizes that it is "put inside," that it is pressed in so that it spreads.
G1470.portee: This parable, contained in this verb, reveals how God acts in history: not through visible and spectacular force, but through the internal and progressive influence of His Spirit. Leaven often represents in the Bible teaching or divine power; hidden as it is, it transforms everything from within.
